done: The hold is lifted at the registrar (or the registry), and the domain resolves again.
estimateChanges: A hold for an unpaid renewal clears in minutes once it is paid. A hold for a complaint or a dispute is the registrar's to lift and can take days.

title: The bare domain or www is not covered by the certificate
what: The https certificate served for the bare domain or for its www host does not name that host.
why: A visitor who types or follows the uncovered address gets a full-page browser warning instead of the site. A link from a business card or a social profile is often the one that is not covered.
fix: Add the missing name to the certificate (most hosts do it from the domain's settings), or point that address at the host that serves it. Then open both addresses in a browser to confirm.
tech: One HEAD request, not followed, to https://<domain>/ and https://www.<domain>/ through the fetcher: the names (subjectAltName, else the common name) come off the connection. When the handshake fails because the certificate does not name the host, Node's error carries the certificate and its names are read from it. A one-label wildcard covers a host. A www that does not exist in DNS is skipped; a certificate that fails for another reason is could-not-check with the code
done: One certificate names both the bare domain and www, and both addresses open in a browser with no warning.
estimateChanges: Adding the missing name to a managed certificate is a setting at the host. A hand-installed certificate has to be reissued with both names.

title: The client is not an owner or admin of a system their site depends on
what: In a system Gaugeline could read, none of the client's addresses (gaugeline.handoff.json) holds an owner or admin role that has been accepted.
why: If you are away, or the relationship ends, the client cannot add a new developer, change a plan or recover the account without asking you, and a lockout can take days to undo while the site's content is out of reach.
fix: Ask a current owner to invite the client's own address as an owner or admin and have them accept it, or promote them if they are already a member. Then run the handoff again.
tech: Read-only, GET only, with the tokens already in the environment: Vercel (GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN: the project, its team and the team's members), Sanity (SANITY_TOKEN: the project's members and their profiles) and Google Business Profile (GOOGLE_BUSINESS_PROFILE_TOKEN: the location's administrators). Each provider's role is mapped to owner, admin, member or viewer; an invitation not yet accepted is not a role. Addresses are compared in lower case and shown only as their first letter and domain. A system whose token may not list members, or whose members' addresses are hidden, is could-not-check for that system alone; no client address in the settings is could-not-check for all
done: The client's own address is an owner or admin of the system, accepted and signed in once, so they can get in and add or remove people without you.
estimateChanges: Minutes in the provider's members page if you are an owner. Longer when the account belongs to a former agency or a teammate who has to be reached to promote anyone.

title: A fulfillment product has variants that cannot be made
what: A Printful product matched to a product on your website has a variant that is not synced.
why: Printful cannot make an order for a variant whose design is not matched to a printable item, so a customer can pay for something that is never printed.
fix: In Printful, open the product and finish syncing the variants listed, or remove them from the store and from the website.
tech: a matched Printful product with at least one sync_variants entry whose synced is false; runs when Printful returned data; the variants are listed by SKU, or by id when there is none, at most 10 and then a count of the rest; an unmatched Printful product is not reported here; with Sanity not read it is reported from the Printful list alone
done: Every listed variant is synced in Printful, or removed from the store and the website.
estimateChanges: The number of variants, and whether the artwork for each exists.

title: A website product is archived in checkout
what: The Stripe product matched to a product on your website is archived.
why: Stripe will not sell an archived product, so the page invites a purchase that checkout turns down.
fix: Unarchive the product in Stripe if it is still on sale, or take it off the website if it is not.
tech: a matched Stripe product with active false; runs when Stripe returned data; an archived Stripe product that nothing matches is not reported (it is not an orphan either); with Sanity not read it is reported from the Stripe list alone; one finding per product with its name and the Sanity and Stripe ids
done: The product is active in Stripe, or off the website.
estimateChanges: Several products archived together are one edit each.

title: A website product is missing from checkout
what: A product published on your website has no matching product in Stripe.
why: A product people can see but checkout does not know cannot be bought: the button fails, or the order never reaches you. That is lost money from the first visitor.
fix: Create the product in Stripe, or save its Stripe id on the website product so the two are linked. If it is not for sale, unpublish it.
tech: a published Sanity product that matchProducts paired with no Stripe product; runs only when both Sanity and Stripe returned data, so a Stripe that was not configured, refused the key or did not answer never makes a product missing; a Stripe that answered with no products at all makes every product missing, and the evidence says so; one finding per product with its name and ids
done: The product exists in Stripe and is linked by id, or is unpublished.
estimateChanges: Setting up prices and tax in Stripe adds time when the product is new there.

title: Website price disagrees with checkout
what: The price on your website (Sanity) is different from the price Stripe charges for the same product.
why: Customers see one price and pay another, which causes abandoned carts, complaints and refunds.
fix: Decide which system owns the price, usually checkout, and have the other read from it. Until then, change one of the two so they agree.
tech: the Sanity product's price against the unit_amount of the matched Stripe product's default_price, both whole minor units (Sanity has no currency and takes Stripe's); compared only when the Stripe currency is known; a default price with no fixed amount (tiered or custom pricing), one that was not read, or a Sanity price with no whole reading in that currency is skipped with a notice; a Stripe product with no default price is stripe-no-price, not a mismatch; the evidence carries both amounts and the rule that matched the pair, and never says which is right
done: The site and checkout show the same price for each product named.
estimateChanges: Deciding which system owns the price comes first. Prices typed into many places are edited one by one.

title: The page sells a plan that is archived in checkout
what: A plan on your page is paired with a Stripe price that has been archived.
why: Visitors can pick the plan, but the price behind it can no longer be used to start a subscription: checkout fails, or an old link keeps charging a price you retired.
fix: Point the page at the plan's current Stripe price, or restore the price in Stripe if it should still be sold. Take the plan off the page if it is gone.
tech: a plan found on its configured page whose matched Stripe price has active false, matched by the configured price id, then the product's gaugelinePlan metadata, then the product name, as the product matcher does; the plan's other comparisons are skipped, since the archived price is the one cause
done: The page points at a current Stripe price, or the plan is off the page.
estimateChanges: Several pages that sell the same plan are one edit each.

title: A plan bills on a different schedule than the page says
what: The page says a plan bills one way (per month, say) and the matched Stripe price bills another (yearly, or every 3 months), or is not a subscription price at all.
why: A customer who expects 49 a month is charged 588 up front, or the other way round. It is the commonest cause of subscription refunds and chargebacks.
fix: Change the page's wording or pick the Stripe price that bills on the schedule the page promises. Create the missing price in Stripe if there is none.
tech: the billing interval written next to the plan's name (per month, /mo, monthly, every 3 months, al mes, mensual, cada 3 meses, and the weekly, yearly and daily forms) against recurring.interval and recurring.interval_count of the matched price; 12 months equals a year and 7 days a week; a card that names two different intervals, or none, is skipped with a notice, not guessed
done: The page and the Stripe price bill on the same schedule.
estimateChanges: A missing price in Stripe has to be created first.

title: A plan's price on the page differs from checkout
what: The price shown for a plan on your page is different from the Stripe price it is paired with, or the page and Stripe disagree about whether tax is included.
why: Customers see one price and are charged another, which causes abandoned checkouts, complaints and refunds.
fix: Decide which price you mean, then change the other so they agree. If the difference is tax, say on the page whether the price includes it.
tech: the first amount written with a currency next to the plan's name, as a whole number of minor units, against unit_amount of the matched price (or its currency_options entry when the page's currency is one of them); a currency that is not one of the price's is a notice, never converted; a plan showing an introductory price or discount is skipped unless introAmount names it; the page's 'tax included' or 'plus tax' against tax_behavior when both say; the evidence shows both amounts and never says which is right
done: The page and checkout show the same plan price, with tax stated on the page if it differs.
estimateChanges: Deciding which price is meant comes first.

title: A field your query asks for is on no document
what: A query in your code asks for a field of a document type, and no published document of that type has it.
why: The field was renamed or never filled in, and the page that asks for it renders empty every time. The schema still declares it, so a type check passes and nobody sees the gap until a customer does.
fix: Open the file and line named, then find what the field is called in your content now (the Studio shows it) and change the query, or fill the field in. Ask Gaugeline again to confirm.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never counted), asking for count(*[_type == T]) and count(*[_type == T && defined(path)]) for each distinct field path, held in a Map from type to a Map from path to an integer; a reference or an array of objects is counted at the field itself (topic, not topic->title); the answer is integers, so no document and no field value is read; a path whose count is 0 while the type's total is above 0
done: The query asks for a field that exists on documents, and Gaugeline finds it.
estimateChanges: Finding what the field is called now, then every query that uses the old name.

title: A document type your query asks for has no documents
what: A query in your code asks for a document type, and the dataset has no published documents of it.
why: Either the type was renamed or the content has not been created yet. Every page built from the query is blank, and its fields are not reported separately because none of them can exist.
fix: Check the type's name in the Studio against the one in the query, or publish the documents. A document that is only a draft does not count.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never counted), asking for count(*[_type == T]) and count(*[_type == T && defined(path)]) for each distinct field path, held in a Map from type to a Map from path to an integer; a reference or an array of objects is counted at the field itself (topic, not topic->title); the answer is integers, so no document and no field value is read; count(*[_type == T]) is 0
done: The type named in the query has published documents.
estimateChanges: A wrong type name is one edit. Documents that were never published need an editor.

title: Two documents share a slug
what: Two or more published documents of one type have the same slug.
why: A slug is the address. Only one document can own it, so a page built from the other cannot be reached, or the site shows whichever the query happens to return first.
fix: Open the documents named by their ids in the Studio. Delete the copy you do not want, or give it its own slug.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never read), projecting only _id, "slug": slug.current and title; one pass puts each id into a Map from the slug as it is, or from the trimmed and lower-cased title, to the ids that have it, and a bucket with more than one id is a group; documents with no slug or no title are left out of that key, a draft id is skipped, and types are grouped apart; a slug shared by two or more ids of one type
done: Each document has its own slug.
estimateChanges: A copy that is already linked from elsewhere needs a redirect.

title: A stated total is not the sum of its parts
what: A document states a number, a total, and the parts it is made of add up to a different one.
why: Content written by a pipeline or a model states a total next to its parts and does not check its own sums. The page then promises a number the parts cannot deliver (a meal plan that says 2,400 calories and contains 1,830), and the customer notices before you do.
fix: Open the document by its id in the Studio and decide which side is wrong: the stated number or a part. If a part is missing because something it links to is not published, the references finding for the same document says which. Fix the pipeline's arithmetic if it keeps happening.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each rule (perspective=published, so drafts are never read); the filter does the comparing, so only ids and whole numbers come back, never a stated number, a part or any other field: the type's document count, the _id of the documents that have no stated number, and the _id of those where stated != coalesce(math::sum(parts), 0); a part that does not dereference is null and math::sum skips it; exact equality on the numbers, and the stated field or a part that is not a number on some document is exit 2 and nothing is reported; stated != the sum of the parts path
done: Each stated total equals the sum of its parts.
estimateChanges: Deciding which side is wrong comes first. A part missing because something it links to is unpublished adds another fix.

title: A document links to something that was never published
what: A document links to other documents, and some of them are not published: they do not exist, or exist only as a draft.
why: A reference to an unpublished document resolves to nothing, so a page built from it shows a gap, or a total that is short. Pipelines create the links and the documents separately and do not check that both were published.
fix: Publish the documents named by their ids, or remove the links to them. If the links are meant to be weak, this is expected and the rule is the wrong one.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each rule (perspective=published, so a draft target counts as missing); for each document of the type, the references at the path are counted, and so are those where defined(@->_id); a document where the two differ comes back as its _id, both counts and the _ref of the missing targets (ids), ten at most; nothing else of the document is projected; an item that has no _ref is not a reference and is not counted
done: Every link points at a published document, or the rule is changed on purpose.
estimateChanges: Several documents that link to the same draft are fixed by publishing that one.

title: A write sets a field no document type declares
what: A patch or create in your code writes a field that no document type in the schema declares.
why: Sanity stores it anyway, so nothing fails. The Studio shows no field for it, so no editor can see or correct it, and a page that reads the field you meant never gets it. It is the usual result of a renamed field.
fix: Open the file and line named. Use the name the schema declares, or declare the field in the schema if the write is right.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; a written field (first path segment) that no document type declares
done: Every field the write sets is declared by the document type.
estimateChanges: Declaring a field is a schema change that also needs a deploy.

title: A create leaves out a field the schema requires
what: A create in your code leaves out a field the schema marks as required.
why: Sanity saves the document, and the Studio then shows it as invalid. A page that assumes the field is there breaks on exactly the documents your code made.
fix: Add the field to the create, or stop marking it required if it is not. A create that spreads another object is not checked for this, because the spread may carry the field.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; a create of a known type, with every key visible, that lacks a required field
done: Each create sets every required field.
estimateChanges: Creates in several routes are one edit each.

title: A reference is written as a plain string
what: A reference field is given a plain string where an object with a _ref is needed.
why: A reference is an object. A string in its place is stored without complaint, but the reference never resolves, so every query that follows it with -> gets nothing.
fix: Write { _type: "reference", _ref: "the document's id" } instead of the string.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; a string literal written to a field the schema declares as a reference
done: Each reference is written as a reference object.
estimateChanges: Existing documents that already hold a string need a one-off fix.

title: A field your GraphQL query asks for is not in the schema
what: A GraphQL query in your code asks for a field that the schema does not have on that type.
why: The server answers the whole query with an error, or leaves the field out, and the page that asked for it renders empty. It is the usual result of a renamed or removed field: the query still compiles, and nobody sees the gap until a customer does.
fix: Open the file and line named, and find what the field is called in the schema now (the schema file, or the GraphQL playground) and change the query. Ask Gaugeline again to confirm.
tech: read from the repository with no request for the documents: .graphql and .gql files and gql tagged templates are read into a field use for each field (its parent type, its path from the operation, its file and line), fragments are resolved by name, and each use is one Map lookup (type name to the Set of its field names) in the schema; the schema is one GET of the endpoint's introspection query with the query in the address (or a file given with --schema); mutations and subscriptions are parsed and counted, and never sent; a field use whose parent type is in the schema and whose name is in neither that type's fields nor, for an interface or a union, the fields of any type it can be
done: Every field the query asks for is in the schema.
estimateChanges: Finding the field's new name, then every query that uses the old one.

title: Orders were paid and no receipt went out
what: More orders were paid in Stripe than the mail provider has sent emails for, in the same window.
why: A customer who paid and got nothing has no receipt, no download link and no booking confirmation, and does not know whether the payment worked. Your application's log says the send succeeded, because it records the attempt; the mail provider records what it accepted and sent.
fix: Open the mail provider's dashboard on the days listed and find the sends that failed or never happened, then fix the code or the sender setup behind them. Send the missing emails yourself from the provider: Gaugeline never resends.
tech: paid Checkout Sessions (payment_status paid, not refunded in full) and the emails Resend lists as sent (not bounced, failed, cancelled, queued, scheduled or suppressed) in the same window are compared in memory with a Map<string, number> keyed by the SHA-256 of the lower-cased recipient, one count per key (a multiset), dropped when the comparison returns; an order takes one email from its recipient's count, and the orders left over are the finding, so unmatched is never negative and more emails than orders is a pass; matching is by recipient across the window, not by day, so an email sent to a different address than the order's shows as unmatched; the evidence is two counts and UTC days, never an address, a name, an order id or a payload
done: Every paid order in the window has a receipt sent, and the missing ones are sent.
estimateChanges: The cause may be the code, the sender setup or the provider, and resending takes care with customers' email.

title: A page that should need a session is handed to anyone
what: A route your code treats as signed-in only returns its page when asked with no session.
why: A route that is missing from the navigation is not a protected route. If the page answers a stranger, anyone who guesses or finds the address (a search engine, a shared link, a guess at /account) can read what a signed-in customer would see: invoices, bookings, names.
fix: Check the session inside the page or the route handler, before it renders or reads anything, and answer 401, 403 or a redirect to sign in when there is none. A middleware matcher that does not list the route does not protect it, so add the route to the matcher or check in the page itself.
tech: probing check, off without --owner-consent: discoverRoutes reads the Next.js app directory (every page and route file is a path, route groups in parentheses are dropped, a bracketed segment is dynamic); a route expects a session when a middleware that looks like a gate has a matcher covering it, or its own file or a layout above it calls auth, getServerSession, cookies or currentUser (the root layout aside); only routes that expect a session and are not dynamic are asked, at most 30, in sorted order, at most 5 at once, each with one anonymous GET (no cookie, no Authorization, no Referer, no query string, redirects not followed); the body is read up to 65,536 bytes to tell a sign-in form (a password field) from a page and is never kept; 401 and 403 are refused, 404 is not found, a redirect to another address is a redirect to sign in, 200 without a sign-in form is handed over (high, or low when the body is empty), anything else is could not check; the routes held in an array in path order and the answers in a Map from path to answer, since answers arrive out of order
done: A request with no session to the route gets 401, 403 or a redirect to sign in.
estimateChanges: Several routes that skip the check, or a middleware that is only partly applied, each need the change.

title: A webhook endpoint is not receiving its events
what: An enabled Stripe webhook endpoint has events older than an hour that were never delivered.
why: Stripe tells your site about a payment through a webhook. If the endpoint is down or answering with an error, the payment happened and your site was never told, so no order is recorded, no file is released and no email is sent.
fix: Open the endpoint in the Stripe dashboard, read the failed attempts to see what it answered, fix the route (or the host behind it), then let Stripe retry or resend the events from the dashboard. Gaugeline never replays or retries them.
tech: GET /v1/webhook_endpoints and GET /v1/events with delivery_success=false from the last 30 days; an event counts against an enabled endpoint that takes its type (or *) when it is older than 1 hour and still has pending deliveries, so two endpoints that take the same type are each told about the same event; the evidence is the endpoint's host (never its path, query or secret), the count and the age of the oldest; nothing from an event's payload is read into a result
done: The endpoint answers the provider's events with 2xx and the failed events are resent.
estimateChanges: The fault may be in the route, the host or the signing secret, and events missed in the meantime have to be replayed.

title: The bare domain and www don't settle on one address
what: Of the bare domain and www, exactly one should answer 200 and the other redirect to it permanently (301 or 308). After cutover, both answer, neither does, or the redirect is temporary.
why: Two live copies split links and ranking between them; a missing one is a dead address for everyone who types it; a temporary redirect tells search engines to keep the old one.
fix: Pick one (most sites use the bare domain or www, either is fine) and redirect the other to it with a 301. Most hosts have a primary-domain setting for this.
tech: GET https://<domain>/ and https://www.<domain>/ through the fetcher, first hop each. Also reported when how either answers changed since the snapshot, with both values
done: The bare domain and www settle on one address with a 301.
estimateChanges: Mail or a certificate on the second name adds a step.

title: The domain's mail records changed at cutover
what: Against the snapshot taken before cutover, the domain's MX records (where its mail is delivered) or its SPF record (who may send as it) are different.
why: A new host's DNS template often replaces the mail records: mail then bounces or goes to an old server, and receipts and confirmations land in spam, with nothing on the site to show it.
fix: Put the old MX and SPF values back unless the move was meant. If it was, list mx or spf under expectedChanges in gaugeline.cutover.json with the reason.
tech: gaugeline cutover --before <file>. MX and TXT (v=spf1) at the domain, compared as sets, so order is not a change. A lookup that failed in either run is could not check, never a change
done: The mail records match the old values, or the change is listed under expectedChanges with a reason.
estimateChanges: Mail that already stopped working means finding what was lost. Records edited at a registrar and a host both need checking.

title: A page from the old site is missing on the new one
what: An address the old site published answers 404 or 410 on the new site, after any redirects.
why: Anyone with the old address (a search result, a link in an email, a bookmark, a printed menu's QR code) lands on an error page, and the page's ranking is lost with it.
fix: Move the page's content to the new site, or add a permanent (301) redirect from the old address to the page that replaces it. Run it again to confirm.
tech: Each path in the old site's content list (the WordPress REST API's published posts and pages, a Wix or Webflow export, or the old sitemap) is requested with GET on the new site, redirects followed. A final 404 or 410 is the finding; a 5xx, a refusal, a password or a timeout is could-not-check for that page.
done: Every page the old site published answers on the new site, either at the same address or through one redirect to its new address.
estimateChanges: A missing page is either content that was not moved (minutes in the CMS if it exists, longer if it has to be written again) or a redirect that was left out. The number of pages decides it.

title: A published Webflow item has no page on the live site
what: The CMS says an item is published, and the address its page should have answers 404 or 410 on the live site.
why: Links, the sitemap and search results point at a page that is not there, and the client's announcement leads to an error page.
fix: Check the collection's template page is published and its address matches the pattern in gaugeline.adapters.json, then publish the site. If the item should not be public, archive it in Webflow.
tech: GET /v2/collections/{id}/items/live for each collection named in the `urls` settings, then one GET of the live address from the pattern (redirects followed). A final 404 or 410 is the finding; any other answer that is not a 2xx is could-not-check for that page. A collection with published items and no pattern, and an item whose slug the pattern cannot use, are could-not-check by name and are not asked.
done: Every published item of the collections you named has a page that answers on the live site.
estimateChanges: A page that is gone for every item of a collection is one template or one address pattern. A single item is a slug that was changed or a page the client switched off. A collection with no pages of its own always shows as could not check, which is expected.

title: The iPhone app banner promotes a different app
what: The page's Smart App Banner (the apple-itunes-app meta tag) names a different app id than the page's App Store link.
why: Safari shows the banner at the top of the page on iPhone, so visitors install whichever app it names, which here is not the one the page links to.
fix: Set app-id in the apple-itunes-app meta tag to the same id as the App Store link.
tech: <meta name="apple-itunes-app" content="app-id=..."> differs from every apps.apple.com/.../id<digits> link on the page
done: The iPhone banner's app-id is the same as the id in the App Store link.
estimateChanges: The banner set in more than one template is one edit each.

title: Nothing on the page can be linked to buy
what: A page shows a price and a buy button, but no button is a link with an address or a submit button in a form with an action.
why: Nobody can share a link to the purchase, search engines see no offer, and if the script fails the page is a brochure.
fix: Make the buy button a link to your checkout or payment link, or a submit button in a form that posts to your cart, and let the script improve it from there.
tech: a price (a currency next to a number in the visible text, or an Offer price in the structured data) and at least one button or link whose text matches buy, add to cart, checkout, get it, purchase or download now; none is an a[href] with an address (not empty, #, javascript:, mailto: or tel:) or a submit button in a form with an action or its own formaction; a link to a hosted payment page (Stripe, Square, PayPal.me) anywhere on the page is a pass; the page is read as sent, so a button drawn by a script is not seen
done: The page has a real link or a form that posts to checkout, and the script only improves it.
estimateChanges: A buy button built entirely by a script means rebuilding that button, and each product page that uses it.

title: A form sends fields the CRM doesn't have
what: A Web-to-Lead form on the page submits field names that are not fields on the Lead object in Salesforce.
why: Salesforce drops what it can't place. The visitor typed it, the form said thanks, and the CRM never got it.
fix: Add the field to Lead in Salesforce and use its name in the form, or remove the input from the form.
tech: The names of every input, select and textarea in each Web-to-Lead form in the HTML (hidden or visible; buttons and files excluded) against the field names and labels of Lead from Salesforce's read-only MCP server (getObjectSchema); Web-to-Lead's own names (first_name, zip, lead_source) are matched to their Lead fields; routing, anti-spam and utm_* names are skipped; custom fields sent by id (00N...) can't be compared and are counted; a form in an iframe or drawn by script is could-not-check
done: Every form field the CRM did not know now exists there, or the input is removed from the form.
estimateChanges: New fields in the CRM need someone with admin rights, and each form that sends them needs the same name.

title: Tracking starts after the form loads
what: The service's tracking code comes after its form in the page, or waits for the page to finish loading while the form is an iframe that loads first.
why: Salesforce documents that this can lose first-touch tracking, the referring site and UTM parameters.
fix: Load the tracking script directly in the page head, before the form, not from a window load handler.
tech: Position of the tracking script after the form in document order (counted over every form, iframe and script element), or inline tracking code started by addEventListener("load"), attachEvent("onload") or window.onload while the form is an iframe; no timing is measured, and code a tag manager moves at run time is not seen
done: The tracking script loads in the page head before the form.
estimateChanges: A tag manager that fires it late is a rule change, not a code change.

title: New leads are arriving without a source
what: Many of the leads created in your CRM since the last run have an empty lead source or campaign field.
why: A lead with no source can't be tied to the ad, email or search that brought it, so the campaign that worked looks the same as the one that didn't.
fix: Make the form send the source: add hidden utm_source and utm_campaign fields, map them to the CRM's lead source or campaign field, and fill the existing records that have none.
tech: Through Salesforce's read-only MCP server (soqlQuery on Lead, newest 200 created since the last run or windowDays ago): leads whose LeadSource, or each field named in sourceFields in gaugeline.crm.json, is null or blank; flagged at 2 or more leads and 10% or more of the sample; evidence is the counts, the field names and up to five record ids, never a name or an email
done: New leads arrive with a source and campaign, and the older records are filled in.
estimateChanges: Several forms each need the hidden fields. Filling in old records is a separate data job.

title: A form has nowhere to put campaign details
what: A form posts leads straight to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden campaign fields.
why: Every lead arrives with its campaign, source and ad click blank.
fix: Add hidden utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and gclid fields, fill them from the address, and map them in the form handler.
tech: A form element posting to Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot or Marketo with no hidden input named utm_*, gclid, a lead source or that service's default mapped field; a visible input does not count; an iframe is another document and is could-not-check
done: The form has hidden utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and gclid fields, filled from the address and mapped in the handler.
estimateChanges: Several forms and a handler that needs a code change each add to it.

title: The page is behind the data it is built from
what: The source (your database or CMS) has newer data than the page shows, or a figure on the page differs from the same figure in the source.
why: The sync works but the visitor does not see it: a cache or a revalidation setting is serving an old copy, so fixing the sync would change nothing.
fix: Look at how the page is rebuilt after the data changes: its revalidate time, an on-demand revalidation that the sync should call, or a CDN that keeps the old copy. The evidence shows the Age header when a cache served it.
tech: for each rule with a source and maxLag in gaugeline.freshness.json, the newest time is read from the source (a one-row query or a Sanity field) and compared with the page's stamp: reported only when the page is older than the source by more than maxLag at every instant the stamp could mean; for each spot check (up to five per rule) the figure at the selector is compared with the source's figure for the page (a one-row query, or the row whose key column is the last part of the page's address) with exact decimal arithmetic and the tolerance given (an amount or a percentage of the source's figure); an unreadable source, stamp or figure is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: The page is rebuilt soon after its data changes.
estimateChanges: An on-demand revalidation call from the sync, a revalidate time and a CDN each need different work.

title: Your domain has no DMARC policy
what: There is no DMARC record at _dmarc.<your domain>, so receiving servers have no instruction for mail that fails SPF or DKIM.
why: Mail pretending to be from you is delivered like any other, and large mail providers increasingly expect a DMARC record from anyone who sends.
fix: Add a TXT record at _dmarc.<your domain>: start with v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<an address you read>, then move to quarantine once the reports look right.
tech: Public DNS only: no TXT record starting v=DMARC1 at _dmarc.<host without www.>. The host is read as given; a parent domain's policy is not looked up
done: A TXT record at _dmarc names a policy and an address you read.
estimateChanges: The address that receives reports has to exist and be watched, which is the ongoing cost.

title: Your domain has two SPF records, which cancels both
what: Two or more TXT records at the domain start with v=spf1.
why: Receiving mail servers treat more than one SPF record as an error and ignore all of them, so your mail is checked as if you had none.
fix: Merge them into one record: one v=spf1, every include from both, one -all or ~all at the end.
tech: Public DNS only: the domain has MX records (not a null MX) and two or more TXT records start with v=spf1 (RFC 7208 §4.5: a permerror)
done: The domain has one SPF record that holds every include from both.
estimateChanges: Each service in the two records has to be checked before the merge.

title: An event at your venue lists a different address
what: An event the page says is at the venue (by the venue's name or id) gives a different street address than the venue's own structured data.
why: Maps and search results send guests to the event's address, so a stale one sends them to the wrong door.
fix: Use the venue's own address in each event's location, ideally by referring to the venue's @id instead of repeating it.
tech: Event location names the LocalBusiness (same name or @id) and its address differs by house number or ZIP
done: Each event lists the venue's own address, ideally by the venue's @id.
estimateChanges: Events entered by hand are edited one by one. One venue record referenced by all of them needs a template change.

title: A click your tracking plan expects isn't reported
what: An element in gaugeline.events.json sends no event when clicked, sends it twice, or sends it without a parameter the plan requires.
why: Tracking breaks quietly when templates change: the report for that menu or button just goes empty, and before-and-after comparisons stop meaning anything.
fix: Restore the click handler or tag for that element, and fill every parameter the plan names (for a menu: link text, destination and parent menu).
tech: Each element a plan line selects (a CSS selector, or every link in nav, header, footer or main; at most 20) is clicked in the rendered page with analytics requests intercepted and never delivered, and dataLayer pushes are read for 1500 ms. One push with the event name and every listed parameter filled passes. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check
done: The click handler or tag fires for that element with every parameter the plan names.
estimateChanges: The element may have been rebuilt, and the tag manager and the code both need checking.

title: A page is missing a fact it should show
what: A fact you declared must appear on a page (mustAppearOn) is not in that page's HTML as it is sent.
why: The page visitors use to decide (the order page, the contact page) leaves out the thing they came for, or shows it only after JavaScript runs, which search engines and assistants may not.
fix: Put the fact in the page's server-rendered HTML. A fact in an image's description only is not visible text: write it out.
tech: for each mustAppearOn path among the pages checked, the fact's declared value is in the visible text, a link or JSON-LD of the HTML as sent (image descriptions don't count, and say so)
done: The fact appears as visible text in the page's server-rendered HTML.
estimateChanges: A fact that only lives in an image needs the text written out, one page at a time.

title: Two of your feeds serve the same posts
what: Two feeds the page advertises list exactly the same item links.
why: Subscribers to one feed get the other's posts (a news feed serving the blog, say), and readers who follow both see everything twice.
fix: Point each feed at its own collection, usually a query or category filter that was copied from the other.
tech: The advertised feeds read for feed-broken (at most 3), compared as Sets of normalised item links: equal and non-empty, in any order. Sharing most items is not a duplicate
done: Each feed serves its own collection.
estimateChanges: A filter copied between feeds is one edit each.

title: The feed this page advertises is not a feed
what: The advertised feed address answers, but with something that is not RSS or Atom, often an HTML page.
why: Feed readers cannot read it, so subscribers get nothing. A framework's catch-all route is the usual cause.
fix: Serve the feed's XML at that address, or point the link rel="alternate" tag at the address that does.
tech: the feed body does not start with an XML declaration, <rss> or <feed>
done: The feed address serves a feed, or the page's link points at the one that does.
estimateChanges: A feed made by a plugin that errors takes longer than correcting a link.

title: The feed this page advertises is too large
what: The feed response is larger than 2 MB.
why: Feed readers and aggregators time out or truncate large feeds, and frameworks such as Next.js do not cache responses over 2 MB, so every request rebuilds it.
fix: Limit the feed to recent items (20 to 50 is typical) and put a summary in each item instead of the full post.
tech: the feed response is larger than 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes)
done: The feed holds recent items only, with a summary in each.
estimateChanges: A feed generated by a plugin may expose no setting for this.

title: The page still shows a prediction for something that already happened
what: A page lists a prediction, a pick or a preview whose event date is already past, and it does not show the result.
why: A prediction for a finished game or a past night looks careless at best, and misleads at worst: visitors act on it and the page loses their trust the next time.
fix: Remove the item or switch it to the result when the event ends. Generate the list from the schedule so an event leaves it by itself, and rebuild or revalidate the page after the result is in.
tech: for each rule with a forecast in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active, each item matching forecast.item (up to 200 per page) has its date read from forecast.date inside it, its own datetime or named attribute, or a time element with a datetime inside it, or the page's Event structured data with the property named in forecast.jsonld; the event is past when it is past at every instant the date could mean (a date alone is over when the whole day is, in the site's time zone; a time is over after forecast.lasts, 3h by default); an item that contains forecast.settled already shows its result and is skipped; no items, a date that cannot be read or an item with no date is could not check; the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: Items for events that already happened are gone from the list, or show their result.
estimateChanges: A list built by hand is edited by hand. One built from the schedule fixes itself but needs code, and a cache needs purging.

title: A form now posts to a different address
what: A form still uses the same service, but posts to a different host than last run.
why: A different host can mean a different account or region with the same service, so entries may land where nobody reads them.
fix: Confirm the new address belongs to your account with that service.
tech: With --since last only: the same form key and provider, with a different action host
done: The form posts to an address that belongs to your account with that service.
estimateChanges: If the change was not yours, finding who changed it comes first.

title: A language version doesn't link back
what: This page's hreflang points at a version in another language, but that version's hreflang doesn't point back.
why: Search engines ignore hreflang pairs that aren't confirmed from both sides, so searchers may get the wrong language.
fix: Give every version the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
tech: page A has <link rel=alternate hreflang> to B, and B (fetched) has none to A (a trailing slash is not a difference)
done: Every language version carries the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
estimateChanges: The number of language versions and whether the links come from one component.

title: Most of this page's HTML is a data payload
what: More than half of the HTML, and over 300 KB, is inline data (JSON, __NEXT_DATA__ or a framework's streamed payload) rather than content.
why: Every visitor downloads data the page may never show, and it delays the first paint on phones.
fix: Send only the fields the page renders. In Next.js, trim what getServerSideProps or a server component passes to client components.
tech: inline data scripts are over 300 KB (307,200 bytes) and more than half the HTML; not reported when html-huge is
done: The page sends only the fields it renders.
estimateChanges: A framework data payload shared by many pages is trimmed in one place. Pages that pass whole records to the browser need one edit each.

title: Your calendar names a time zone it doesn't describe
what: Events in your .ics calendar use a TZID, but the file has no VTIMEZONE section for it.
why: The iCalendar standard requires the description. Some calendar apps fall back to UTC or the guest's zone without it, and show the wrong hour.
fix: Export the calendar with time zone definitions included, or add a VTIMEZONE for each TZID the events use.
tech: a DTSTART or DTEND TZID has no matching VTIMEZONE component (RFC 5545 §3.6.5)
done: The calendar carries a VTIMEZONE for each TZID its events use.
estimateChanges: Software with no export option for this needs a different export.

title: Images are requested at an enormous width
what: An image is offered or requested 3840 pixels wide or more, wider than almost any screen shows it.
why: Phones and laptops may download a 4K-wide picture to show it a few hundred pixels across, which wastes data and slows the page.
fix: Cap the widths your image component generates (for Next.js, deviceSizes and imageSizes in next.config) and set the sizes attribute.
tech: a srcset candidate with a w descriptor, or a w= parameter, of 3840 or more
done: The image component generates widths up to a sensible cap and sets the sizes attribute.
estimateChanges: One shared image component is one edit. Hand-written srcsets are edited one by one.

title: None of the images on this page are described
what: The page has images, and not one has alt text that says what it shows.
why: Screen reader users hear nothing about any picture, and search engines have no words to index the images by.
fix: Give each meaningful image an alt that says what it shows. alt="" is right for decorative images, but a page where every image is decorative is rare.
tech: every img has a missing, empty or whitespace-only alt
done: Each meaningful image has an alt that says what it shows.
estimateChanges: Writing good descriptions takes time per image, and images inside CMS content are edited one by one.

title: Some images are very large files
what: An image on the page is over 500 KB.
why: Large images are the most common reason a page is slow on a phone, and a slow page loses visitors before it loads.
fix: Resize the image to the size it is shown at and export it as WebP or AVIF, or serve it through an image CDN or your framework's image component.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Length header is over 512,000 bytes; a server that sends no Content-Length gives no finding
done: The images are resized to the size they are shown at and served as WebP or AVIF.
estimateChanges: A site that serves originals needs an image component or CDN set up, then each image needs checking.

title: Images still load from an old WordPress site
what: Images on the page are served from /wp-content/uploads/, usually left over from a WordPress site the new site replaced.
why: When the old WordPress install or its host is switched off, every one of these images breaks at once.
fix: Move the images into the new site's own media library or asset folder and update the addresses.
tech: img src or srcset candidates under /wp-content/uploads/
done: The images live in the new site's own media library and no address points at the old site.
estimateChanges: The number of images, and links inside CMS content that still name the old address.

title: A language version of this page is missing
what: The page says (through hreflang, the sitemap or your language settings) that it has a version in another language, but that version returns an error or redirects to the homepage.
why: Visitors who switch language land on an error or on the homepage, and search engines drop the alternate from results.
fix: Publish the missing version, or remove it from the page's hreflang links and the sitemap. Pages meant to exist in one language only can be excluded in gaugeline.languages.json.
tech: an expected twin (hreflang, sitemap xhtml:link or the configured prefix, subdomain or parameter) answers 4xx or 5xx, or redirects to / or a language root; at most 5 versions are fetched
done: The missing language version is published, or removed from the hreflang links and the sitemap.
estimateChanges: Translating the page is the cost. Removing the link is minutes.

title: Some links go through a link shortener
what: Links leave the page through a shortener or redirector (bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, a /redirect?url= address) instead of linking directly.
why: Visitors can't see where the link goes before they click, the redirect adds a delay, and if the shortener expires or is blocked the link breaks.
fix: Link straight to the destination. Social icons in the footer are a common place for these.
tech: a[href] on bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, buff.ly, ow.ly, tinyurl.com, goo.gl, rebrand.ly, is.gd, cutt.ly, shorturl.at, tiny.cc (or a subdomain), or a /redirect, /out or /go path with a url= style parameter holding an http(s) address; footer links count too
done: Links go straight to their destination.
estimateChanges: Social icons in the footer are one edit. Wrapped links inside posts are one each.

title: A listing shows a different address
what: The street number or ZIP code on your Google, Yelp or Apple listing is not the one on your site.
why: Maps sends people to the address on the listing. After a move, or with a typo, guests arrive at the wrong door.
fix: Correct the address in the listing's own dashboard, or on the site if the listing is the right one.
tech: the house number and the 5-digit ZIP code are read from both addresses and each one both sides state must be equal; street names are not compared; the site's address is the text fact "address" in gaugeline.facts.json, else the LocalBusiness address in structured data
done: The listing and the site show the same address.
estimateChanges: Each listing is edited in its own dashboard, and an address change that needs verification can take days.

title: A listing doesn't know about a holiday closure
what: Your site announces a day you are closed, such as Thanksgiving or Christmas, and a listing still shows its normal hours for that day.
why: People check the listing on the day. If it says you open at 4 on a day you are shut, they come anyway.
fix: Add the closure to the listing's special hours in its own dashboard (Google Business Profile: Special hours; Yelp for Business: Holiday hours).
tech: closures on the site are dates in LocalBusiness openingHoursSpecification (validFrom and validThrough, opens and closes both 00:00) and dates or fixed US holidays within 40 characters of the word "closed" in the pages read, from today in the venue's time zone up to 60 days ahead; a listing is missing one when its special hours (Google Business Profile, Yelp) do not mark that date closed; sources that give no special hours (Google Maps, Apple) are reported as could not check
done: The holiday closure is in the listing's special hours.
estimateChanges: Each listing (Google, Yelp, Apple) is its own dashboard.

title: Your llms.txt sends assistants to pages that don't work
what: Links in /llms.txt return an error (4xx or 5xx) or redirect to a different site.
why: llms.txt is a short guide for AI assistants to your most useful pages. A dead or off-site link is the page they quote, or fail to.
fix: Update the links to the pages' current addresses, or remove the ones that no longer exist.
tech: links in /llms.txt answer 4xx or 5xx, or redirect off-site
done: Every link in llms.txt loads.
estimateChanges: A llms.txt generated by a plugin is fixed at the source.

title: Your llms.txt gives assistants an old phone number, address or hours
what: The phone number, street address or opening hours in /llms.txt disagree with the page's structured data.
why: Assistants quote llms.txt directly. An old number or old hours there is what someone hears when they ask if you're open tonight.
fix: Update llms.txt to match the structured data (or the other way round, whichever is wrong). Generate both from one source if you can.
tech: hours, telephone or address in /llms.txt differ from the page's LocalBusiness JSON-LD
done: llms.txt gives the same phone number, address and hours as the structured data.
estimateChanges: Generating both from one source removes the drift but needs a template change.

title: Some buttons open an email instead of a form
what: A contact button ("Talk to an expert", "Get a quote") opens one person's email program instead of a form.
why: The enquiry skips your CRM: it lands in one inbox with no campaign details, nobody else sees it, and visitors without an email program set up can't send it at all.
fix: Point the button at a form or a booking page that sends the enquiry to your CRM, and keep the email address as a plain fallback.
tech: a[href] starting mailto: with an address, whose text is a contact call to action (contact, talk, speak, get in touch, email us, book, quote, demo and similar) and not an address itself; one finding per page; the link's styling is not visible to Gaugeline
done: Each button opens a form or booking page whose enquiry reaches the CRM.
estimateChanges: A form and its CRM connection are built first if there is none, then each button is repointed.

title: A block that shows entries of a type is empty
what: A block on another page (an "insights" strip, a team row) is meant to show entries of a document type, shows none, and entries of that type are published.
why: Pages that embed a type break when it changes: a renamed field or a stricter filter empties the block, the page still loads, and it is a page nobody opened.
fix: Compare the block's query with the type as it is now (renamed fields, a filter on a field older documents lack). If the block is meant to be empty for now, take it out of gaugeline.model.json.
tech: For each dependent in gaugeline.model.json: the page is read with GET and the entries are the selector's matches. With none, count(*[_type == T && (filter)]) over published documents (GET) says whether there is anything to show; a type with no published documents is not reported. With --since last and a block name, the evidence adds how many entries the saved run listed. A page that cannot be read is could not check
done: The block shows entries again, or is empty on purpose and listed as such.
estimateChanges: A renamed field in the query, a filter on a field older documents lack and a type that is now empty each fix differently.

title: Documents still hold a field the schema no longer has
what: Published documents have a value in a field that was removed from the schema: usually a leftover from before a rename, a merge or a clean-up.
why: The Studio no longer shows the field, so nobody can see or fix what is in it, but a query or a page may still read it, and the old value can be wrong or private.
fix: Decide for each field: if a page or query still needs it, put it back in the schema; if it moved to another field, copy the values across and then unset the old one with a one-off migration.
tech: GROQ cannot list the keys a document has without sending the document, which Gaugeline never does, so the fields looked for are named: the fields of the schema file in previousSchema that the current schema no longer has, and the fields under retired in gaugeline.model.json. For each, count(*[_type == T && defined(field)]) over published documents and the first three ids in id order (GET). A field the current schema still has is never reported. No value is requested or shown. Without a schema file, or with no field named, the check is could not check
done: Each field no longer in the schema is put back, copied across and removed, or left on purpose.
estimateChanges: The number of documents and fields. Unsetting values is a data migration that needs a backup first.

title: The menu changed since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, links in the header or footer menu were added, removed, moved to another parent, renamed or reordered.
why: A menu restructure changes many links at once and every page still loads, so nothing else reports the page that lost its only link.
fix: Check each change was meant. A removed link whose page now has no other link needs one, or a redirect if the page is gone.
tech: With --since last only. A link is its region, parent item and destination. Same destination under a new parent is moved; same identity with new text is renamed. A removed link whose destination has no inbound link from the pages read is high. On a first run (no saved menu yet): could not check
done: Each menu change since the last run was meant, and a page that lost its link has another or a redirect.
estimateChanges: The count of changes since the last run.

title: The footer isn't the same on every page
what: A page's footer links differ from the footer most of the pages read have, or a footer link gaugeline.nav.json marks as required (privacy, terms, contact) is missing.
why: A footer that differs on one template usually means that template was missed in a change; a missing privacy or terms link can be a legal problem.
fix: Use one footer for every template, and add any required link that is missing.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Footer destinations on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the most common set is the reference. Required links match a footer link's text or path, case-insensitively
done: Every page shows the same footer with every required link.
estimateChanges: Templates that each carry their own footer are edited one by one.

title: Menu items go to the homepage
what: Links in the menu or header point at the homepage but are labelled as something else, such as Services or Contact.
why: Visitors who click Services land back on the homepage and think the page is missing. It usually means a menu item was added with no link.
fix: Point each menu item at its own page, or remove it until the page exists.
tech: a nav or header a[href] resolving to / whose text (or aria-label) is not Home or the site's name
done: Each menu item goes to its own page, or is removed until the page exists.
estimateChanges: Items whose pages are not built yet need those pages first.

title: Pages in the sitemap that no page links to
what: Addresses the sitemap lists that none of the pages read link to, in their menus, footers or text.
why: Visitors can only reach them from search or an old bookmark, and search engines treat a page nothing links to as unimportant.
fix: Link to each page from its section's menu or a related page, or take it out of the sitemap if it is gone.
tech: With --since last or a gaugeline.nav.json (it reads the run's other pages). Same-site sitemap addresses (one level of index) against every link on the checked page and the run's other pages (4); the checked page itself is excepted. A page linked only from a page not read is reported too: the evidence says how many were read
done: Each page in the sitemap has a link from its section or a related page, or is out of the sitemap.
estimateChanges: Many orphans from one section are one menu change.

title: The mobile menu is missing links the desktop menu has
what: The page has a separate mobile menu, and some destinations in the desktop header menu aren't in it.
why: Most visitors are on a phone: a page missing from the mobile menu is missing for them.
fix: Add the missing links to the mobile menu, or build both menus from one list.
tech: The separate mobile menu's destinations (gaugeline.nav.json regions.mobile, or a [data-mobile-menu], #mobile-menu or .mobile-menu element) against the header's. A menu toggle whose menu isn't in the HTML is could not check: it is built at a phone width, which needs a rendered read (not on yet)
done: The mobile menu has every link the desktop menu has.
estimateChanges: Two menus kept by hand are edited twice. One list feeding both needs a code change.

title: The page still shows an old copy after an edit
what: With a content source connected, this Next.js page is still a cached copy made before its document last changed, more than 10 minutes after the change.
why: Editors publish a fix and visitors keep seeing the old version, so the fix looks broken.
fix: Revalidate the page when its document changes (an on-demand revalidation webhook from the CMS), or lower its revalidate time.
tech: Next.js sites with a content source (branch 30) only, otherwise unchecked: x-nextjs-cache or x-vercel-cache HIT or STALE with an Age header, the copy's age older than the document's last change, and the change more than 10 minutes ago. Without an Age header nothing is reported
done: An edit in the CMS shows on the live page without a redeploy.
estimateChanges: An on-demand revalidation webhook is set up in the CMS and the app. A revalidate time is one line but gives slower updates.

title: The share picture doesn't load
what: The og:image the page names answers with an error, or can't be reached.
why: When someone shares the page, the preview card shows no picture, or none at all, on the day you most want it to look right.
fix: Point og:image at an image that loads on the live domain (open the address in a browser to check), and use a full https:// address.
tech: One probe of the og:image address (HEAD, then GET on 405/501), counted in the images budget; 4xx, 5xx or no answer is a finding. No og:image is og-image-missing's to report
done: The og:image address loads on the live domain over https.
estimateChanges: One shared SEO component is one edit. Pages that set it by hand are edited one by one.

title: Shared links may show no picture
what: og:image is a relative address (like /previews/landing.webp), not a full https:// address.
why: Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack and iMessage need a full address. With a relative one, shares of the page show no picture.
fix: Write og:image as a full address, including https:// and the domain. Most frameworks have a site URL setting for this.
tech: og:image does not start with http:// or https:// (protocol-relative // addresses are flagged too)
done: og:image is a full address with https and the domain.
estimateChanges: One site URL setting in the framework usually fixes every page.

title: Shared links point at a different page than search engines see
what: The page's og:url (the address social apps use when it is shared) differs from its canonical tag.
why: Likes and shares are counted against one address while search engines rank another, and a share can open the wrong page.
fix: Set og:url to the same address as the canonical tag. Both usually come from one SEO component.
tech: og:url and <link rel="canonical"> differ by scheme, host, path or query (a trailing slash is not a difference)
done: og:url equals the canonical address.
estimateChanges: Both come from one SEO component on most sites.

title: This page is heavy to load
what: The HTML plus the images Gaugeline sampled add up to over 3 MB, and that is a floor: unsampled files come on top.
why: On a phone connection a page this heavy takes many seconds and costs visitors data.
fix: Start with the largest files in the evidence: resize and compress images, and trim the HTML's inline data.
tech: HTML bytes plus the Content-Length of sampled images (the files the run already requested) is over 3 MB (3,145,728 bytes); no extra requests are made
done: The page loads within the size budget, with the largest files resized or trimmed first.
estimateChanges: The number of large images and how much of the HTML is inline data.

title: A listing has fewer items than last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a repeated list on a page (products, posts, people, events) has fewer items, with the ones that are gone where items carry links.
why: A shop page with 7 products instead of 12 still looks complete: items drop out when a feed, a filter or a category breaks, and nobody counts.
fix: Check the items that are gone were removed on purpose. If they weren't, look at what feeds the list. A listing meant to shrink goes under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json.
tech: With --since last only. A list is a ul or ol with 3 or more items, or an element marked data-list, in the main content; it is named by its data-list value or the heading before it. For a paginated list only the first page is compared, and the evidence says so. On a first run: could not check
done: The missing items are back in the list, or the page is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: Finding what feeds the list, which may be a query, a filter or a deleted entry.

title: A page lost its structured data since the last run
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, a structured-data type that a page had (Product, Recipe, Event, Article) is no longer there.
why: Search results show rich listings (prices, ratings, dates) only from structured data; when a template or plugin change drops it, the page reads the same and the listing quietly goes plain.
fix: Put the markup back where the template lost it, or list the page under expectedChanges in gaugeline.pages.json when it was removed on purpose.
tech: With --since last only. Types are read from JSON-LD @type and microdata itemtype, with the schema.org prefix dropped. One finding per page, naming every type gone. On a first run: could not check
done: The structured data is back on the page, or the page is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: A template that lost it affects every page that uses the template.

title: The site shows two different handles for one payment service
what: With no payment details set, the pages checked show two or more different handles for the same service.
why: At most one of them is right. Customers can't tell which, and some pay the other one.
fix: Keep the right handle everywhere, and set it in gaugeline.payments.json so Gaugeline checks against it.
tech: Only without gaugeline.payments.json: a Zelle, Cash App, Venmo or PayPal handle with more than one distinct value (compared case-insensitively; Zelle phones by digits) across the pages checked
done: One handle is shown everywhere and is set in gaugeline.payments.json.
estimateChanges: Handles typed into several pages are one edit each.

title: The page shows placeholder images
what: Images on the page come from a placeholder service such as placehold.co, dummyimage.com or picsum.photos.
why: Visitors see grey boxes or random stock photos where the real product or team picture should be.
fix: Upload the real images and point the img tags at them.
tech: img src on placehold.co, placehold.it, placeholder.com, via.placeholder.com, dummyimage.com, picsum.photos, placekitten.com, placebear.com, loremflickr.com, fakeimg.pl, placeimg.com, lorempixel.com (or a subdomain)
done: The real images are uploaded and the img tags point at them.
estimateChanges: The number of images, and whether the real ones exist yet.

title: The page still has placeholder text
what: The page shows unfinished copy: lorem ipsum, TODO or TBD, a [bracketed placeholder], or a title or main heading such as Untitled, Staging or Test.
why: Visitors see an unfinished site, and search engines may show the placeholder in results.
fix: Replace the placeholder with the real copy. Search the CMS for "lorem", "TODO" and "[" before publishing.
tech: main content text matches "lorem ipsum", TODO/TBD/FIXME or [insert ...]-style brackets (code and pre ignored), or the whole title or h1 is one of "untitled", "untitled page", "untitled document", "new page", "page title", "title", "test", "test page", "testing", "staging", "staging site", "my site", "my website", "site title", "home page title" (English lists)
done: The placeholder is replaced with the real copy.
estimateChanges: Copy that has not been written is the real cost.

title: Your address takes several jumps to load
what: The address you entered redirects more than once before the page loads.
why: Each jump slows the first visit and can weaken how search engines credit the page.
fix: Point every redirect straight at the final address.
tech: more than one 3xx hop on the entered URL
done: Every redirect points straight at the final address.
estimateChanges: Rules in the host, a CDN and the app each need checking.

title: A breadcrumb ends on a different page
what: The last item of a page's breadcrumb structured data points at an address other than the page's own canonical.
why: The trail should end where the visitor is. One that ends elsewhere usually means the breadcrumb was copied from another page.
fix: Make the last ListItem's item the page's canonical address, or leave the last item's URL out.
tech: the highest-position ListItem has a URL that differs from the canonical (or the page address) by scheme, host, path or query; needs a gaugeline.schema.json
done: The last ListItem of the breadcrumb is the page's canonical address.
estimateChanges: A shared breadcrumb component is one edit.

title: Structured data refers to something that isn't there
what: A structured data reference ({"@id": ...}) points at a node that is not defined on the page or on the other pages checked.
why: Search engines can't follow the reference, so whatever it stands for (the publisher, the author, the organization) is lost.
fix: Define the node the reference names (usually on the homepage), or correct the @id to the one you use.
tech: an object with only an @id resolves (after normalisation) to no @id defined on the sampled pages
done: The node the reference names is defined, or the @id is corrected.
estimateChanges: Structured data written by a plugin may not allow either change.

title: Pages redefine your organization instead of referring to it
what: Pages other than the homepage define the Organization or WebSite again, with its properties, instead of referring to the one node by its @id as your schema guide says.
why: Copies drift: one page gets an old logo or phone number, and search engines see several organizations where there should be one.
fix: On every other page, write {"@id": "<the configured id>"} where the Organization or WebSite is needed, and define it once on the homepage.
tech: an Organization or WebSite node with properties beyond @id and @type on a page other than / (needs organizationId or websiteId in gaugeline.schema.json)
done: Every other page refers to the Organization by @id and the homepage defines it once.
estimateChanges: Structured data written by several templates or plugins each need the change.

title: A page is missing structured data its template requires
what: A page that matches one of your schema guide's templates (for example /blog/*) lacks a type the guide requires there, such as Article or BreadcrumbList.
why: Rich results for that kind of page depend on the type, and one template that drifted usually means every page built from it did.
fix: Add the missing type to the template's structured data component.
tech: the most specific matching template's require list has a type missing from the page's JSON-LD (@type anywhere, @graph included); common subtypes count (an AboutPage is a WebPage, a BlogPosting an Article); needs templates in gaugeline.schema.json
done: The template's structured data includes the required type.
estimateChanges: Several templates that share the component are fixed once.

title: A third-party script is new, or lost its integrity attribute
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, the page loads a third-party script it did not load before, or one that had an integrity attribute no longer has it.
why: Any script on a checkout page can read what customers type. Knowing exactly which ones load, and noticing a new one, is what PCI DSS 11.6.1 asks of a payment page.
fix: Confirm the script was added on purpose and by whom. Remove it if not. For one you keep, add its integrity attribute so a changed file stops loading.
tech: With --since last only. Third-party means a host outside the page's registrable domain. A script is its host and path with no query string; the integrity attribute is present or not. Scripts that went away are not reported. On a first run: could not check
done: Each script that appeared since the last run is one you or the client added on purpose, and a script that lost its integrity attribute has it back.
estimateChanges: Finding out who added a script is the unknown. A tag manager can load many scripts that this page's code never names.

title: A security header sends less protection than before
what: Against the last run saved with --since last, one of these headers is gone or weaker: Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy.
why: These headers switch browser protections on. They vanish when a host, a CDN or a framework setting changes, and the site looks the same.
fix: Find what changed in the hosting or header settings and put the header back, or confirm the change was meant.
tech: With --since last only. The final response's headers. Reported: a header gone; Strict-Transport-Security with a smaller max-age or without includeSubDomains or preload; X-Content-Type-Options no longer nosniff; X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and the Cross-Origin policies with a less strict value; a Permissions-Policy feature removed or given a new origin. On a first run: could not check
done: The header is sent as it was, or the change was meant.
estimateChanges: Usually one line in the host's or the framework's header settings. A CDN or proxy change can drop several at once.

title: Your sitemap lists pages on a different address
what: Every entry in the sitemap uses a different host than the site, for example a staging domain or the other of www and the bare domain.
why: Search engines ignore sitemap entries for a host the sitemap does not belong to, so the sitemap does nothing for this site.
fix: Generate the sitemap with the site's public address. In most frameworks this is a site URL or base URL setting.
tech: every sitemap entry's host differs from the page's host
done: The sitemap lists pages on the site's public address.
estimateChanges: A site URL setting is one line. A hand-written sitemap is edited by hand.

title: Search engines can't find a list of your pages
what: There is no sitemap at /sitemap.xml, and robots.txt does not say where one is.
why: Without a sitemap, search engines find pages only by following links, so new or deep pages take longer to appear.
fix: Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml (most site builders and frameworks can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full address to robots.txt.
tech: /sitemap.xml is not a 200 sitemap and robots.txt has no Sitemap: line
done: A sitemap loads at /sitemap.xml and robots.txt names it.
estimateChanges: A framework or plugin that generates one is a setting. Without one it is built from the page list.

title: Your sitemap lists old addresses that redirect
what: Pages listed in the sitemap answer with a redirect (3xx) instead of the page.
why: A sitemap should list the final address of each page. Redirecting entries make search engines do extra work and can keep the old address in results.
fix: List each page at the address it redirects to. This often follows a move to https, to www, or to a new URL scheme.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 3xx
done: Each sitemap entry is the address its page redirects to.
estimateChanges: A move to https, www or a new URL scheme changes every entry at once, and the sitemap is regenerated.

title: The same structured data is on this page twice
what: A schema.org type is described both in JSON-LD and as microdata (itemtype) on the same page.
why: Search engines see two descriptions of one thing, which can disagree, and may pick the wrong one or ignore both.
fix: Keep one: usually the JSON-LD, and remove the itemscope and itemtype attributes from the theme or plugin that adds microdata.
tech: a schema.org @type in JSON-LD is also a microdata itemtype
done: The page carries one copy of the structured data, usually the JSON-LD.
estimateChanges: A plugin or theme that adds microdata has to be configured or removed, which can change other pages.

title: A page does not say what it should for the current switch
what: You said what a page must tell visitors while a feature is on or off ("order at the bar" while pre-orders are off), and the page does not say it.
why: A visitor who reaches the page learns nothing: no explanation, no other way to order. They are left guessing whether the site is broken.
