fix: Show the message from the same switch that turns the feature off, so the two cannot disagree. If the evidence says a cache served the page, purge it after the switch changes.
tech: for each switch in gaugeline.switches.json, the page text for the current state (whenOff.pageSays while off, whenOn.pageSays while on) is read from the page as sent, without JavaScript, with hidden elements left out; the phrase is matched case-insensitively and ignoring accents, spacing and punctuation, in the page's own language when the phrase is given per language (a bilingual site's other-language pages are read through gaugeline.languages.json); a page that answers 404, a source or a page that cannot be read is could not check (the link checks report dead pages); the evidence adds the Age and Cache-Control headers when a cache served the page
done: The page shows the message from the same switch that turns the feature off.
estimateChanges: A cache needs purging, and each page that reads the switch needs the same source.

title: A tracking rule points at something that no longer exists
what: A Tag Manager trigger waits for a page address, link, form or element that no page on the site has, so its tags never fire.
why: Tag rules outlive the pages they were written for: a download or form trigger tied to a retired address goes quiet, and the report just shows fewer leads.
fix: Point the trigger at what the site uses now (the nearest match is in the evidence), or delete it and the tags that only it fires.
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json (no Tag Manager account is used). Page address conditions are compared with the pages read, their same-site links and the sitemap; click and form conditions (Click URL, ID, Classes, Text, Element; Form ID, Classes, Text, URL, Element) with the elements of the pages read. A trigger type, variable or comparison it doesn't read, a custom event, or a trigger limited to pages the run didn't read is listed under could not check
done: Each rule fires on something the site still has, or is deleted with its tags.
estimateChanges: The number of rules in the container, and who owns the tags that only they fire.

title: Two tags send the same event at the same moment
what: Two Tag Manager tags that aren't paused send the same event to the same place on the same trigger.
why: Every lead, download or sale is counted twice, so conversion numbers and the ad bidding built on them are wrong.
fix: Keep one of the tags and pause or delete the other (usually the copy).
tech: The container export named in gaugeline.tags.json, read without requests. GA4 event tags are the same when the event name and the measurement ID match; any other tag type when its type and every setting match. Paused tags are left out
done: One of the two tags is kept and the other is paused or deleted.
estimateChanges: Which copy is the real one has to be decided by someone who knows the account.

title: This page isn't set up for phone screens
what: The page has no viewport meta tag, so phones show it zoomed out as if on a desktop screen.
why: Visitors have to pinch and zoom to read anything, and Google treats the page as not mobile-friendly.
fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the page's head.
tech: no <meta name="viewport"> anywhere in the document
done: The page head has a viewport meta tag.
estimateChanges: A template shared by every page is one edit. Pages built with different templates are one each.

title: A title tag isn't what the plan says
what: The title tag the preview sends isn't the one the plan gives the page.
why: Someone edited the page, or the template overrode it, and the title the plan chose for search is gone.
fix: Set the page's title to the plan's, or update the plan if the change was deliberate.
tech: The page row's Title Tag against the HTML title, compared trimmed, case-folded, whitespace collapsed, quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix counts. No title in the HTML is reported with a hint that it may be set by JavaScript
done: Each page's title equals the plan's, or the plan is updated.
estimateChanges: Pages edited by several people need the change in one place.

title: An H1 isn't what the plan says
what: The page's first H1 isn't the one the plan gives it.
why: Usually a content change nobody recorded; the heading the plan chose for the keyword is gone.
fix: Set the H1 to the plan's, or update the plan.
tech: The page row's H1 against the first h1 in the HTML, compared like titles; a page with several H1s is noted
done: Each page's H1 equals the plan's, or the plan is updated.
estimateChanges: Deciding which side is right comes first.

title: A planned #section isn't on the page
what: A plan row with a #section points at an id that isn't on the page.
why: Links to the section land at the top of the page, and the plan's section was never built.
fix: Add the section with that id, or change the row to the id the page uses.
tech: The row's fragment against every element id in the HTML the preview sends
done: Each planned #section has an element with that id on the page.
estimateChanges: A section that was never built is the full cost of building it.

title: An old address takes more than one redirect
what: An old address takes two or more redirects to reach its page.
why: Each hop costs visitors time, and search engines follow only so many before giving up on passing signals.
fix: Redirect the old address straight to the final page. A server that adds a trailing slash first counts: redirect the old address's own form.
tech: More than one 3xx in the hop list the fetcher records; the trail is in the evidence
done: Each old address redirects once, straight to the final page.
estimateChanges: Rules in the host and in the app each need checking.

title: A menu item and its page are named differently
what: A menu item matches no page by name, and exactly one page shares a distinctive word with it.
why: The menu and the page plan disagree on the name, so the page's title, H1 and keyword may not be what visitors click.
fix: Use one name in both places, or record the difference on purpose.
tech: Distinctive words are five letters or more, not health, healthcare, medical, service(s) or management. Exactly one page name with one of them; the evidence gives both labels and both lines
done: The menu item and the page use one name.
estimateChanges: A name that is on purpose different is recorded rather than changed.

title: A menu item links to a page that still needs building
what: A menu item matches a page row whose Status says Need Page.
why: The menu will link to a page that hasn't been built: at launch it is a 404 in the navigation.
fix: Build the page before launch, or leave the item out of the menu until it exists.
tech: The matched row's Status cell against /need(s) page/i. Skipped, with a note, when the plan has no Status column
done: The page is built before launch, or the menu item is left out until it exists.
estimateChanges: A page that is not written yet is the real cost.

title: Two rows in the plan have the same title tag
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same title tag.
why: Search engines show the title in results; two pages with one title compete with each other and neither looks like the answer.
fix: Write a title that says what is different about each page.
tech: Title Tag cells compared trimmed, whitespace collapsed, lower case, with curly quotes and dashes straightened; a brand suffix is part of the title. Empty cells are left out
done: Each planned page has a title that says what is different about it.
estimateChanges: Writing good titles takes time per page.

title: Two rows in the plan have the same H1
what: Two or more rows of the plan plan the same H1.
why: The H1 tells visitors and search engines what the page is about; two pages with the same heading read as the same page.
fix: Give each page a heading that names its own topic.
tech: H1 cells compared the same way as titles. Empty cells are left out
done: Each planned page has a heading that names its own topic.
estimateChanges: Writing good headings takes time per page.

title: A slug misspells its own heading
what: A word in a page's address is one or two letters away from a word in the same row's page name or H1, such as credentialling for Credentialing.
why: The address is permanent once it is indexed and linked; fixing a typo later means a redirect, and until then the page looks careless in results.
fix: Use the heading's spelling in the slug (the corrected path is in the evidence) before the page is built.
tech: Words of 5+ letters in the last path segment, not in the row's page name or H1, within Damerau distance 1 of a heading word (2 for words of 8+ letters). Plural and tense endings (s, es, ed, ing) and listed British/American pairs are excused; accents are folded. One finding per row
done: The slug uses the heading's spelling.
estimateChanges: Easy before the page is built. After it is linked or indexed it also needs a redirect.

title: Two pages in the plan target the same primary keyword
what: Two or more pages of the plan have the same Primary Keyword, so they will compete for one search before a line of code is written.
why: Search engines show one page per query from a site; two pages chasing the same term split their links and usually both rank worse than one would.
fix: Give each page its own primary keyword, or merge the pages into one.
tech: Primary Keyword cells compared trimmed, lower case, spaces collapsed, quotes straightened and a trailing full stop removed; no stemming (singular and plural differ). Empty, n/a, none, tbd, - and bracketed placeholders are left out. A page and its anchor rows count once. Groups sorted by a Primary Volume column when there is one
done: Each page has its own primary keyword, or the competing pages are merged.
estimateChanges: Merging pages means content and redirect work.

title: Some old addresses in the plan's notes aren't settled
what: A notes column read with --legacy-from mentions a legacy page in words instead of by its address, or asks whether it should redirect, so no redirect can be checked for it.
why: Old addresses that rank keep their traffic only with a 301 to the right new page. A note nobody resolved is a redirect nobody will build.
fix: Put the old address in the note ("301 legacy /old-page here.") or decide and write it, then run the plan check again.
tech: Sentences in the --legacy-from columns containing "legacy": one that says 301 but names no path (no-path), or one with a path that starts with Confirm, contains whether or ends with a question mark (unconfirmed). One finding listing every line
done: Each old address in the notes is written as a path or decided, and the plan check passes.
estimateChanges: Someone who knows the old site has to say what each note means.

title: A printed link to a page now lands on the home page
what: A printed link to a page deeper than the home page now lands on the home page.
why: The classic lazy redirect after a restructure: the visitor who scanned for the menu has to find it again.
fix: Redirect the printed address to the page that replaced the one it was printed for, and add its expectedDestination to the register.
tech: No expectedDestination; the printed path isn't / and the trail ends on /
done: The printed address redirects to the page that replaced its original, and its expectedDestination is in the register.
estimateChanges: Several printed addresses each need their own redirect.

title: A printed address loses its tracking tags
what: A printed address's utm_ (or other configured) parameters are gone by the time it reaches its page.
why: Scans of that table tent or flyer can't be counted: the campaign looks like it did nothing.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect.
tech: Parameters on the printed URL whose names start with a tag prefix (utm_ by default) and are missing from the final address
done: The redirect passes the query string on, and the scan reaches the page with its tags.
estimateChanges: A short-link service may need its own setting.

title: The same product is in Printful more than once
what: Two or more Printful products have the same name, or the same external id.
why: An order for the product can be made from either copy, with different designs or prices, and the shop only knows one of them.
fix: Keep one product, delete the rest in Printful and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: Printful store products grouped by normaliseName, then by external id (trimmed, exact), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and an external id group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's id, up to 10 and then a count; a blank external id or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Printful returned data
done: One product is kept in Printful and the website points at it.
estimateChanges: Orders attached to the copies need care before they are deleted.

title: The same product is on the website more than once
what: Two or more published Sanity products have the same name, or the same non-empty SKU.
why: The shop has the same product twice, so a price, a photo or a stock figure can be right on one copy and wrong on the other, and a link to checkout may be saved on only one of them.
fix: Keep one product, unpublish or delete the rest in Sanity and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: published Sanity products grouped by normaliseName, then by SKU (trimmed, lower-case), each in one pass into a Map; a product in a name group and a SKU group is listed once, in the name group; one finding per group with every copy's _id, up to 10 and then a count; an empty SKU or a name that normalises to nothing is never a group; runs only when Sanity returned data
done: One product is kept in the website's content and the others are unpublished or deleted.
estimateChanges: Links to the copies need a redirect.

title: The same product is in Stripe more than once
what: Two or more active Stripe products have the same name once case, spacing and punctuation are ignored.
why: Until one record is the real one, nothing can say what checkout should charge: the copies may carry different prices, and the website may point at any of them.
fix: Keep one, archive the rest in Stripe and point the website at the one you keep. Gaugeline does not choose which.
tech: active Stripe products grouped by normaliseName in one pass into a Map; one finding per group listing every copy with its id and default price, up to 10 and then a count; archived products are not counted as copies and are named in the finding when their group also has active ones; names that normalise to an empty string are never grouped; runs only when Stripe returned data
done: One product is kept active in Stripe and the others are archived.
estimateChanges: Payment links and subscriptions on the copies have to be moved first.

title: An email still has template variables in it
what: A rendered email still holds a variable that was never filled in, such as {{order_id}}, {% if paid %}, {name} or [object Object].
why: The customer reads "Order {{order_id}} is confirmed" or "Hi undefined", which looks broken and hides the one detail (which order, which booking) they opened the email for.
fix: Pass the missing value to the template, or delete the variable. For a preview that was exported before the data was merged, export the email from the real send path or with sample data.
tech: Handlebars and Mustache {{ }} and {{{ }}}, Liquid {% %}, ERB and EJS <% %>, JavaScript ${ }, JSX and message {name} and {props.name}, [object Object], Mailchimp *|MERGE|* tags, undefined and NaN as words, and null alone or after a greeting; read in the text a recipient sees and in attributes (style and script bodies and comments are left out, JSON-LD is not), and in the .txt beside it; one finding for each file, at the first line
done: The re-exported email has a real value wherever the template has a variable, and no placeholder is left in the HTML or the text version.
estimateChanges: A variable the email build never receives is one fix. A template that renders before its data arrives needs the render moved.

title: An image in an email will not load in an inbox
what: An image in a rendered email is on a relative path, on localhost or a private address, or on plain http://.
why: A relative or local image is a broken box in every inbox, and many mail apps block or warn about plain http images, so the logo or the product photo is missing exactly where the customer is looking.
fix: Serve the images from your live site over https and write their full addresses into the email (https://example.com/mail/logo.png), or attach them inline.
tech: img[src] in the rendered HTML with no scheme, with http:, or with an http(s) address on a local or private host (the list is the one email-relative-link uses); cid: and data: images are not read; the address is shown without its query; one finding for each email, at the first line
done: Every image in the email is an https:// address on a public host, or travels inside the message (cid:).
estimateChanges: Images served from one setting are a single change. Images pasted in by hand are edited one by one.

title: The domain's registration runs out soon
what: The domain's registration expires in under 30 days (fix soon) or under 7 (fix first), by the date the registry publishes.
why: When a domain lapses the site and every email address on it stop working, and a lapsed name can be bought by someone else. The first you hear of it is usually the owner on the phone.
fix: Renew it at the registrar the finding names, and turn on automatic renewal. If the client holds the account, send them the date and ask them to renew, or ask for access so it is not left to a card that may have expired.
tech: RDAP, the registries' public replacement for WHOIS: IANA's bootstrap file (data.iana.org/rdap/dns.json) names the registry's server for the TLD, then one GET of /domain/<name> there, no key. The date is the earliest "expiration" event; the registrar is the name in the registrar entity. Whole days from the run's clock in UTC. A registry with no RDAP service, a rate limit, an outage, a platform address (name.vercel.app) or a registry that hides its dates is could-not-check with the reason, never a guess; WHOIS is never read
done: The domain is renewed at the registrar, with a registration date a year or more ahead and automatic renewal on.
estimateChanges: Minutes when you hold the registrar login. Days when the client or a former agency does, because someone has to be reached to approve the renewal.

title: An access token expires soon
what: A GitHub or Vercel token you set up for Gaugeline reports an expiry date within 21 days (fix soon) or 7 (fix first), or in the past.
why: When a token lapses, whatever uses it stops with no warning: a deploy hook, a content sync, a scheduled job. It usually shows up as a site that quietly stops updating.
fix: Create a replacement with a later date, update everything that uses the old one, then revoke the old one. A token with no expiry is listed as "no expiry reported", not as a problem.
tech: Only tokens you put in GAUGELINE_GITHUB_TOKEN or GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN are asked. GitHub: one GET of /rate_limit, reading the GitHub-Authentication-Token-Expiration response header. Vercel: one GET of /v5/user/tokens/current, reading expiresAt. Only the date is kept, and the token is never printed, logged or put in a result. A token whose provider reports no date is could-not-check (no expiry reported); nothing is created or revoked
done: A new token is created with a date well ahead, the deploy or sync that uses it is updated, and the old one is revoked.
estimateChanges: Minutes for one token. Longer when it is copied into several places (a CI secret, a hosting setting, a teammate's machine) and nobody remembers where.

title: A Vercel project runs a Node.js version Vercel is retiring
what: A Vercel project you listed in gaugeline.renewals.json uses a Node.js version that Vercel has announced it will stop supporting (or already has).
why: Once Vercel retires a version, new deployments of the project can fail to build, and a site nobody touched for months stops being deployable the day someone needs to fix something.
fix: Set the project's Node.js version to a current one (Project Settings, then Node.js Version, and the engines field in package.json), deploy a preview and check the site before promoting it.
tech: GET /v9/projects/<name> on Vercel with GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN, reading only nodeVersion. The version's major is looked up in packages/core/src/data/vercel-node-runtimes.json: a dated list of the versions Vercel has announced for retirement, each with the page that says so. A version that is not in the list has no announced retirement and is not a finding. Under 7 days or past is high, under 90 days medium, further out low
done: The Vercel project builds and runs on a Node.js version Vercel supports, set in the project's settings and in package.json.
estimateChanges: Changing the setting takes a minute. Moving a project across two majors can turn up packages that no longer install or code that relied on old behaviour, so test it on a preview first.

title: The freelancer is the only owner or admin of a system the client depends on
what: A system has exactly one owner or admin that has accepted, and it is one of the freelancer's addresses (gaugeline.handoff.json). Two addresses listed together under sameAs count as one person.
why: One person is the single way in. If their login is lost, their account is closed or they are unreachable, nobody can add anyone, and the client has to wait for them.
fix: Make a second person an owner or admin: the client first, and ideally a teammate you trust as well. Then run the handoff again.
tech: Read as client-not-admin does. Owners and admins who have accepted, and who are not an API token, are counted by person: the addresses a person is listed under in sameAs share one key. Exactly one such person, whose address is in freelancerEmails, is the finding. A system whose members could not be read is could-not-check, never a pass
done: At least two different people can let others in or out of the system, and one of them is the client.
estimateChanges: Minutes in the provider's members page. It needs the client to accept an invitation, which can take as long as they take to open an email.

title: A system the site depends on lives in a personal account
what: The project that serves or feeds the site belongs to one person's account, not to a team or organisation.
why: A personal account is one person's login. It has no list of members to add the client to, it cannot outlive that person's access, and it often belongs to the freelancer who set the site up, so the client's site is tied to a login that is not theirs.
fix: Create a team or organisation owned by the client (or by both of you), move the project into it, and give the client's own address the owner role. Then run the handoff again.
tech: Vercel: the project's accountId. An id that begins with team_ is a team; any other is a personal account, whose one owner is the token's own user (GET /v2/user). Other systems report a personal account only when their API says so. A project whose owner cannot be told apart is could-not-check
done: The project lives in a team or organisation account that the client owns, and it has been moved there without a break in the site.
estimateChanges: Moving a project between accounts can change its address, its environment variables and its domain settings. Plan an hour for a small site, and check the site afterwards.

title: The page's HTML is different on every request
what: Visiting the page twice, a few seconds apart, gives different HTML even after nonces and CSRF values are ignored.
why: A page that is different on every visit cannot be cached, so the host builds it again for every visitor. On a Next.js site that is the usual cause of a hosting bill that grows faster than the traffic, and it makes the page slower as well.
fix: Find the first difference in the finding. If it is a time, a counter or a random id, print it in the browser instead of when the page is built, or move it behind a cache lifetime. If it comes from a CMS query, ask whether that part has to be fresh on every visit.
tech: Two GETs of the page about 3 seconds apart, the first being the one the check already made, both with no cookies (a variant a cookie would choose is the one a first-time visitor gets). Before comparing, volatile values are blanked by a fixed table: nonce attributes and 'nonce-' sources, the value of csrf-token meta tags and hidden CSRF fields, Cloudflare's scrambled emails; whitespace is collapsed. The finding quotes the first differing word in each body. A cookie whose name looks like an experiment (ab_test, variant, bucket) is named in the evidence. Pure string comparison: the same two bodies give the same answer. Only with --cost or gaugeline cost; pages listed under "pages" in gaugeline.cost.json are visited too
done: Two visits a few seconds apart give the same HTML, so the host can keep one copy and serve it, and the hosting bill stops growing with every visitor.
estimateChanges: Often an hour to find the value (a clock, a counter, a random id) and move it to the browser or behind a longer cache time. Longer when the page is built from a CMS query that includes it.

title: Hosting usage jumped
what: A usage figure the hosting provider reports for yesterday is more than a set multiple (2 by default) of its average over the 14 days before.
why: A site can quietly multiply its hosting bill when a page stops caching or a loop starts. The jump shows up in the usage figures days before the invoice, which is the time to fix it, and to tell the client before they find out.
fix: Open the provider's usage page for the metric named, and look for the day it started: a deploy, a page that began changing on every visit (see output-changes-every-request), a new image or API call. Fix the cause, then run again tomorrow.
tech: Read-only, one GET of the provider's usage with the token in the environment: Vercel's billing charges (GAUGELINE_VERCEL_TOKEN; Vercel has no read-only token type, so use one scoped to the team). Each service and unit is a metric, and the billed cost one more, summed by UTC day in thousandths (integers). The latest complete day before today by the injected clock is compared with the mean of the days before it (window and multiple in gaugeline.cost.json): flagged when more than the multiple, ignoring a day under one whole unit and a metric with no earlier usage. Sanity's usage has no documented read API, so it is could-not-check. Not applicable to a site on Wix, Squarespace, Webflow or Framer: a fixed plan. No token is could-not-check; the page checks still run
done: Yesterday's usage is back within the multiple of its recent average, or the jump is explained (a campaign, a launch) and the plan covers it.
estimateChanges: An hour to find the cause in the provider's usage page (a page that stopped caching, an image loop, a crawler). Longer if the fix is a plan change the client has to approve.

title: A JavaScript library the site serves has a published advisory
what: Gaugeline reads the JavaScript files a page loads, finds the version of jQuery, jQuery UI, Lodash, Moment.js, Bootstrap or AngularJS in them, and lists the published advisories that name that version, with the version that fixes each.
why: Libraries in an old theme or plugin stay at the version they were installed at, and advisories are published about versions long after. This is a list of facts: which version is served and which advisories name it. Whether an advisory matters for this site depends on how the site uses the library, which Gaugeline cannot see, and it does not say.
fix: Look at where the file comes from: the theme, a plugin, a package in the project or a CDN address. Update it to a version past the fixes the finding lists, or take the library out when nothing uses it, then test the pages that use it. If it is bundled into code you cannot change, tell the client who maintains it.
tech: Only with --libraries. The script files the page's own HTML names (script src, same site or another, at most 20, each fetched once with GET, never any address the page does not name) are read as text and never run; at most 2 MiB of each is read and searched, and each script is reported once per run, on the first page that names it. The version comes from a banner comment, a version string in the code or the library's own file name (jquery-3.5.1.min.js, or jquery.min.js under a /jquery/1.12.4/ or lodash@4.17.21 folder; a query string and a folder with other files are never a version), the file's own text first, and only from a whole banner or code shape, never a sentence in a comment. It is compared with packages/core/src/data/library-advisories.json: for each advisory, the affected versions and the page that publishes it, with a verified flag that is false until someone has compared the entry with its page, and a finding says so while it is false. A finding shows the library, its version, the script's address (with no query), and each advisory with its id, a short description and the fixed-in version, never script text beyond the version. A library recognised by name with no version, a script that cannot be read or is longer than what is read, and minified files with no library name or version are could-not-check. A library bundled into one minified file with its banner removed is not seen. The same files give the same findings
done: The libraries the finding names are on versions past the fixes the advisories list, or the client has decided with the developer who knows the theme that they stay; running Gaugeline again shows the versions served.
estimateChanges: An hour for a library the theme loads from a file you can swap. A day or more when the library is bundled into an old theme or plugin and the code that uses it has to be tested on the newer version.

title: WordPress, a plugin or a theme is older than its current release
what: Gaugeline reads the WordPress version a page shows (the generator tag, or the version on the files WordPress loads from wp-includes) and the version of each plugin and theme in the addresses of the files the page loads, and compares them with the current releases the public wordpress.org API lists.
why: Most WordPress updates fix something, and a site that falls behind keeps the problems the updates fixed. This states which versions are shown and which are current; it does not say a site can be attacked. A site that hides its versions is not reported as up to date: Gaugeline says it could not check.
fix: Take a backup, update on a staging copy if there is one, then update WordPress, the plugins and the theme the finding names, and look at the pages that use them. A premium plugin that is not in the wordpress.org directory is updated from its own vendor and is listed as could-not-check here.
tech: Only with --wordpress. The version of WordPress is the generator meta tag (WordPress 6.4.2), else the ?ver= on the core files under /wp-includes/ (the emoji and block-library files); a plugin's or theme's version is the ?ver= on its files under /wp-content/plugins/<slug>/ or /wp-content/themes/<slug>/, read as a release number written with dots (2.1.3, 5.8, 1.0.0-beta2) and never a date, a hash or a timestamp, which are cache-busters; a number that is WordPress's own (what WordPress writes when a plugin gives none) is not the plugin's, and neither is the number on a file the plugin bundles from another project (a vendor, lib or fonts folder, or a file such as font-awesome, bootstrap or swiper), which is that project's. What a page declares is only what its files say: a version newer than the directory's current release is could-not-check, not current. A plugin whose files carry more than one number, or none, is could-not-check. The current releases are one GET each to https://api.wordpress.org/core/version-check/1.7/ and https://api.wordpress.org/plugins/info/1.2/ (themes/info/1.2/ for a theme) with the slug the page shows, no key and nothing sent, at most 15 plugins and 15 themes for the whole run, shared by every page (the rest are listed as could-not-check with their number). A plugin or theme not in the directory (a premium or custom one) is could-not-check. A page the run reaches on a site that is not WordPress is skipped. Versions are compared as whole numbers in four parts (5.10 is after 5.8), and each component is reported once per run, on the first page that shows it.
done: WordPress, the plugins and the theme the finding names are on their current release (or the client has decided with the developer why one stays), and running Gaugeline again shows the new version numbers.
estimateChanges: An hour when the site has a staging copy and the updates are clean. A day or more when a plugin is years behind, the theme is customised, or nobody has tested updates on this site before.

title: The site's REST API lists its users to anyone
what: Gaugeline asks the site's REST API for its list of users the way a visitor's browser can, with no login, and reports when it answers with users.
why: The list gives each author's display name and the slug that is often also the login name, so anyone can learn who the accounts are before guessing passwords. It is on by default in WordPress, which is why it is common, and closing it costs a site very little. This is a fact about what is listed, not a sign of a break-in.
fix: Restrict the users route to logged-in users: most security plugins have the setting, or a short snippet in the theme's functions.php removes it for visitors. Check the author archive pages the theme shows, and that no plugin or app on the site needs the list public.
tech: Only with --wordpress. One GET of the REST root the page names in its api.w.org link (the same site only), /wp-json/wp/v2/users?per_page=100&_fields=id, with no key; if /wp-json/ answers 404, one GET of /?rest_route=/wp/v2/users (a site with plain permalinks). Only the id is asked for, so no name or slug is sent back, and only how many users were listed is kept and shown. A 401, 403 or 404 from both routes, or an empty list, is not exposed. Any other answer, an answer that is not a list, or a request that fails is could-not-check. The route is a documented, public REST route, so it is not a probing check under rule 14; it is still off unless --wordpress is given. Pages of a site that is not WordPress are skipped, and the site is asked once per run.
done: The REST API's list of users answers a visitor with no login with an error or an empty list, and running Gaugeline again finds no users listed.
estimateChanges: Minutes with a hardening plugin or a small snippet in the theme. A site whose app or booking plugin needs the list public takes longer, because it has to be given another way first.

title: Fulfillment lists a different price
what: A synced Printful variant's retail price is different from the price Stripe charges for the product.
why: Anything that reads Printful's price (a storefront sync, an invoice, a packing slip) shows customers a different number from the one they paid.
fix: Decide which price you mean, then change the other so the two agree, or have Printful's retail price follow checkout.
tech: each synced sync_variants.retail_price of the matched Printful product against the unit_amount of the matched Stripe product's default price, both whole minor units; compared only when the variant's currency is known and equal to Stripe's (a different currency is a notice, never converted); a variant with no retail price, or a Stripe default price with no fixed amount, is skipped with a notice; one finding per product listing up to three differing variants and both match rules
done: Fulfillment and checkout list the same price.
estimateChanges: Deciding which system owns the price comes first.

title: No default price in checkout
what: An active Stripe product that is matched to a product on your website has no default price.
why: Anything that asks Stripe for the product's price (a payment link, a checkout session, a price comparison) finds nothing, and the product cannot be bought or compared.
fix: In Stripe, open the product and set one of its prices as the default, or archive the product if it is no longer sold.
tech: a matched Stripe product with active true and default_price null, whether or not it has other prices; the evidence says how many prices it has; archived products and Stripe products with no Sanity partner are not reported
done: The product has a default price in Stripe, or is archived.
estimateChanges: Several products are one edit each.

title: A plan's free trial differs from checkout
what: The page promises a free trial that the matched Stripe price does not give, or Stripe gives a trial the page never mentions.
why: Someone who signs up for a free trial and is charged today, or who is surprised by a trial that hides when the first bill comes, files a dispute.
fix: Make the page and the Stripe price agree on the trial's length, or take the promise off the page.
tech: a trial of N days, weeks or months written next to the plan's name (7-day free trial, prueba gratis de 7 dias) against recurring.trial_period_days of the matched price (a month is 28 to 31 days); a trial set when checkout is created (subscription_data) is not visible on the price, so confirm there before changing the page
done: The page and the Stripe price agree on the trial length, or the promise is removed.
estimateChanges: A trial changed in Stripe affects customers who are already on it.

title: A query does not leave drafts out
what: The filter of a query in your code does not leave drafts out.
why: With the published perspective in the client that is safe. If anything runs the query with drafts included (preview mode, a token with the wrong perspective), unpublished content reaches a visitor.
fix: Add !(_id in path("drafts.**")) to the filter, or make sure the client always asks for the published perspective. Gaugeline cannot see the client, only the query.
tech: read from the repository with no request: the query's filter is parsed and does not require !(_id in path("drafts.**")) (or match "drafts.*") in an && chain
done: The query filters out drafts, or the client always asks for the published perspective.
estimateChanges: The same query pattern repeated in many files is one edit each.

title: Two documents share a title
what: Two or more published documents of one type are called the same thing, ignoring case and spaces around the title.
why: Different addresses, same name: usually content that was duplicated and not moved, which splits search results between two pages. It can also be two real pages that need different names.
fix: Open the documents named by their ids. If one is a copy, delete it and redirect its address; if both are real, rename one so a visitor can tell them apart.
tech: one GET of the query endpoint for each document type (perspective=published, so drafts are never read), projecting only _id, "slug": slug.current and title; one pass puts each id into a Map from the slug as it is, or from the trimmed and lower-cased title, to the ids that have it, and a bucket with more than one id is a group; documents with no slug or no title are left out of that key, a draft id is skipped, and types are grouped apart; a title shared by two or more ids of one type that do not all share one slug
done: Each document has its own title, or the copy is deleted with a redirect.
estimateChanges: A copy already linked from elsewhere needs a redirect.

title: A query fetches a field the code never reads
what: A query in your code asks for a field, and nothing that receives the result ever reads it.
why: Every field you ask for is data your visitors download and your server waits for, and nobody sees it. Over a few months a query collects fields from pages that changed, and the page gets slower for content it never shows.
fix: Open the file and line named and take the field out of the query, unless something Gaugeline cannot read (a script, another repository) uses it. A query listed as could not follow was left alone on purpose: its result goes somewhere Gaugeline cannot read, so none of its fields were reported.
tech: read from the repository with no request and no key: each groq template, defineQuery call and gql template is read into a tree of the fields it returns, named by alias ("slug": slug.current is slug), and the TypeScript compiler's symbols follow the result through variables, await, destructuring, props passed to components, map callbacks, returns and spreads into JSX props; a field counts as read when a property access or a destructuring reads its alias on a value that came from the query, held in a Map from query to the Set of aliases read, so unused is the aliases projected minus the aliases read; _id, _type, _key and _rev are never reported; a query whose result escapes (JSON.stringify, a function from a package, a field read by a name only known at run time) is listed as could not follow and none of its fields is reported
done: The field is out of the query, unless a script or another repository uses it.
estimateChanges: Gaugeline cannot see other repositories, so someone has to check before the field is dropped.

title: A write edits published content directly
what: A patch, createOrReplace or delete in your code has no drafts handling: its id is not a drafts. id.
why: It changes the published document directly. An editor who has unpublished changes in the Studio can lose them, or have them published by the next write.
fix: Patch the draft (the id with "drafts." in front) and let an editor publish, or leave it as it is if writing straight to the published document is what you want.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; an id that does not start with drafts. and is not built by something named like a draft helper
done: The write patches the draft and an editor publishes, or writing to the published document is recorded as intended.
estimateChanges: Routes that write in several places each need the change, and editors need a publish step.

title: Two routes write the same field
what: Two or more routes in your code write the same field of the same document type.
why: Each route assumes it owns the field. When their rules differ, the last one to run wins, and the value drifts without anyone changing it on purpose.
fix: Decide which route owns the field and have the others call it, or accept it if they are meant to share it.
tech: read from the repository with no request at all: the TypeScript compiler reads client.patch(...).set(...), create, createOrReplace, createIfNotExists, delete, transaction chains and raw mutations arrays into a Map from each written field to the kind of its value (a plain string, an object with _ref, anything else), which is compared with the schema file given by --schema (the output of sanity schema extract); no mutation is sent, and the module cannot import an HTTP client; a Map from type.field to the routes that patch or replace it, and an entry with more than one route; a patch of a field that several types declare is not attributed to a type
done: One route owns the field and the others call it, or the sharing is recorded as intended.
estimateChanges: Deciding which route owns it comes first.

title: A webhook endpoint is switched off
what: A Stripe webhook endpoint has the status disabled.
why: Stripe sends a disabled endpoint nothing. If your site still depends on it, payments are made and the site is not told.
fix: If the endpoint is still needed, enable it in the Stripe dashboard (Stripe may have disabled it after days of failures, so read its last attempts first). If it is not, delete it so the list says what is live.
tech: GET /v1/webhook_endpoints; an endpoint whose status is disabled is a finding, whatever it takes; the evidence is the endpoint's host only
done: The endpoint is enabled in the Stripe dashboard, or deleted if it is no longer needed.
estimateChanges: Stripe disables an endpoint after days of failures, so the failures need reading first.

title: The certificate no longer covers a name it did
what: The https certificate after cutover lacks a name the one before covered (www, a subdomain), or there is no certificate where there was one.
why: Visitors on the name that dropped off see a security warning instead of the site.
fix: Add the missing name to the new host's certificate (most hosts add www as a separate domain).
tech: Names from subjectAltName, a wildcard covering one label. A new issuer or a renewed date alone is not a change
done: The new certificate covers every name the old one did.
estimateChanges: Most hosts add www as a separate domain, and each extra name is one more.

title: The domain's DNS records changed at cutover
what: Against the snapshot taken before cutover, the domain's DMARC record, a DKIM key (for the selectors in gaugeline.cutover.json) or its address records (A, AAAA) are different.
why: A lost DKIM key or DMARC record breaks mail authentication quietly; new address records are the cutover itself, worth confirming they point where the new host says.
fix: Check each value against what the new host and your mail provider publish. List a change that was meant under expectedChanges in gaugeline.cutover.json.
tech: TXT at _dmarc.<domain> (v=DMARC1), TXT at <selector>._domainkey.<domain>, A and AAAA at the domain; sets compared. A lookup that failed in either run is could not check
done: Each changed record matches what the new host and the mail provider publish, or is listed under expectedChanges.
estimateChanges: The number of records, and records edited at both a registrar and a host.

title: An old address takes more than one redirect to reach its page
what: An address from the old site reaches its page on the new site only after two or more redirects, or never settles because the redirects loop.
why: Every extra redirect is another round trip for the visitor, and search engines pass less on through each one and may stop following a long chain.
fix: Point the old address straight at the page's final address with a single 301, and make the slash, www and https rules agree with it.
tech: The redirects of the GET to each path on the new site are counted from the fetcher's record of every hop. One redirect is accepted; two or more, or a loop, is the finding. A trail that ends in 404 is migration-page-missing instead.
done: Each old address that moved reaches its new address in a single redirect.
estimateChanges: Usually one rule changed in the host's redirect settings. A chain made of a framework's trailing-slash rule plus a manual redirect needs the manual one pointed at the final address.

title: A page's title changed in the move
what: The title the old site gave a page (its name in the list, and the old page's <title>) does not match the new page's <title>, og:title or first heading.
why: The title is what a search result shows. A title that changed by accident, because a CMS field was not mapped, can cost clicks and rankings the page had earned.
fix: Put the old title back in the new page's title field, or leave the new one if you changed it on purpose.
tech: Both titles are lower-cased with accents, punctuation and spacing removed; they match when equal or when one holds the other as whole words, so adding or dropping the site's name is not a change. The list's title is compared with the new <title>, og:title and first <h1>; the old page's <title> with the new <title> and og:title. With neither an old title nor an old page, the page is could-not-check.
done: Each page that moved has the title it had, or a change you made on purpose.
estimateChanges: One field per page in the CMS. A title built from a template that was mapped wrongly changes them all at once.

title: A page's canonical address changed in the move
what: The old page named an address as its canonical, and the new page names a different one (or none), and neither is the address the page now lives at.
why: The canonical tells search engines which address to keep. One that points at the blog index, the home page or an address that redirects asks them to drop the page.
fix: Make the new page's canonical the address it is served at. If it moved, that is its new address; the old address should redirect to it.
tech: Paths are compared (the host is left out, since a preview and the live site differ), ignoring a trailing slash and case. The new canonical must equal the old canonical's path or the path the redirects ended on. Needs the old page: with --old, the old site's own address; a page with no old canonical is skipped.
done: Each page's canonical is the address it had, or the address the page now lives at.
estimateChanges: One setting in the framework or the SEO plugin's replacement, then a rebuild. A canonical built from the wrong base address changes every page.

title: A page lost a structured data type in the move
what: The old page had structured data of a type (Article, FAQPage, Event, Product, Recipe, LocalBusiness, BreadcrumbList) that the new page no longer has.
why: Structured data is what earns a page its rich result in search: the FAQ dropdown, the event date, the star rating. Without it the page appears as a plain link.
fix: Add the missing JSON-LD to the new page's template, filled from the page's own content, and test it with a rich results tester.
tech: The @type of every JSON-LD node (an @graph read through) and every microdata itemtype, on the old and the new page. Types that describe the whole site (WebSite, WebPage, Organization, Person, ImageObject, SearchAction) are left out. A type the old page had and the new one lacks is the finding; a new type is not. Needs the old page: with --old, the old site's own address.
done: Each page still carries the structured data types it had (Article, FAQPage, Event, Product and so on).
estimateChanges: A type the new build never wrote means adding the JSON-LD to the page template and filling its fields from the CMS. One template covers every page of its kind.

title: Work saved in the Webflow CMS is not on the live site
what: A collection item was saved as ready (not a draft) and has never been published, or it was changed after it was last published, so the live site still shows the old version or none.
why: The client believes the change is out. Customers see the old price, the old opening hours, or no page for the event they were told about.
fix: In Webflow, review the staged items and publish the site. If an item should not go out yet, set it back to draft so it is not mistaken for finished work.
tech: GET /v2/collections/{id}/items (the staged list) for each collection: isDraft false, isArchived false, and lastPublished absent (staged) or more than 2 seconds earlier than lastUpdated (changed). Drafts and archived items are never reported. Ids, slugs and dates only: no field is used for this.
done: Every item the client saved is published, or is a draft on purpose, and a run of Gaugeline lists none that is staged.
estimateChanges: Publishing is one click in Webflow, but it publishes the whole site, so check what else is waiting before you do. Allow longer where the client has to approve the wording first.

title: Some AI assistants can't read your site
what: robots.txt stops one or more known AI crawlers from reading the home page. Gaugeline says which, and whether the block names them or comes from a rule for every crawler.
why: People ask assistants about a business before they open its site. Blocking AI crawlers is a fair choice; blocking them by accident means assistants answer from old or second-hand information.
fix: If the block is on purpose, there is nothing to do. If it comes from a Disallow: / meant for a staging site, remove it, or add groups for the assistants you want to allow.
tech: known AI user-agent tokens (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json) are disallowed / by robots.txt
done: The assistants you want can read the site, or the block is recorded as on purpose.
estimateChanges: A block set in a firewall or a CDN rather than robots.txt is found by looking at those settings.

title: The store lists the app under a different name
what: The name the App Store or Google Play shows for a linked app differs from the name you expect.
why: A renamed or replaced app can mean the link points at an old listing, or at someone else's app.
fix: Check the link points at the right listing. If the app was renamed on purpose, update the expected name.
tech: the store's app name differs from the expected app name (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored); only runs when an expected name is set
done: The link points at the right store listing, or the expected name is updated.
estimateChanges: Renaming the app in the store is a review by the store, which takes days.

title: A downloadable file is on a public asset address
what: A page links to a file (pdf, zip, epub, mp3, mp4, docx or xlsx) on a public asset store and shows no price, or the link is a terms, privacy or policy page.
why: That is fine for a brochure or a menu. It becomes a problem the day the file is something a customer bought, because anyone with the address can open it.
fix: If the file is free, nothing to do. If it will ever be sold, serve it from a download route that checks the purchase and hands back a short-lived signed link.
tech: a[href] to a file with a sold file type on a public asset store host, on a page with no price, or whose link text is terms, privacy or policy; one finding per page; the file is never requested; the query string is not printed; a signed address with an expiry is a pass
done: The file is served from a route that checks the purchase and hands back a short-lived link, or is left public on purpose.
estimateChanges: A free file needs nothing. A file that will be sold means building the route and moving the file.

title: The site wouldn't let Gaugeline read the page
what: The page answered with a refusal (401, 403, 429, 503 with Retry-After) or a bot-challenge page instead of its content.
why: A firewall or bot protection is in front of the site. That isn't a broken site, but it can also stop search engines' and AI assistants' crawlers, and nothing else could be checked.
fix: If the site should be readable by crawlers, allow them in the firewall or bot-protection settings. Gaugeline never retries or disguises itself to get through.
tech: The final answer for the page is 401, 403, 429, 503 with a Retry-After header, or a 200 under 60 words with a known challenge marker (Just a moment, Attention Required, cf-chl, a captcha form). Every check that needs the page is then listed as could not check; only robots.txt and DNS checks run
done: The site lets crawlers read the page, or the block is accepted as on purpose.
estimateChanges: A firewall or bot-protection setting on a host you do not control is a support request.

title: The page doesn't say which address is the real one
what: There's no canonical tag.
why: Copies of the page with tracking parameters can be treated as separate pages.
fix: Add a self-referencing canonical tag.
tech: no <link rel="canonical">
done: Each page has a canonical tag that names its own address.
estimateChanges: One shared SEO component is a single edit.

title: A page of changing numbers does not say when they were updated
what: A page under one of your freshness rules shows no update time at all, in the place you named or in its structured data.
why: Without a stamp nobody can tell fresh numbers from stale ones, and neither can Gaugeline: a sync can stop and the page gives no sign.
fix: Print the time the data was last updated on the page, from the same record the numbers come from (a time element with a datetime attribute, or dateModified in the structured data), then point the rule at it.
tech: for each rule with a stamp in gaugeline.freshness.json that is active (in the months of activeWhen, in the site's time zone), the page as sent without JavaScript has no element matching the selector with a datetime, content, named attribute or text, and no property of that name in its structured data; a stamp that is there but cannot be read is not reported here (data-stale lists it as could not check); a rule that is not active is listed as could not check, not passed
done: The page prints when its numbers were last updated, from the same record.
estimateChanges: Several pages with changing numbers each need the stamp.

title: Your Sanity content can be read by anyone
what: The Sanity dataset your images come from answers queries without a token.
why: That is fine for a blog, and a risk the day someone adds a form or an order type to it: everything in it is readable by anyone who looks.
fix: If nothing in it is private, nothing to do. Otherwise make the dataset private in sanity.io/manage and give the site a read token.
tech: Project and dataset read from cdn.sanity.io image addresses; one GET to <project>.api.sanity.io with the query {"count": count(*), "types": array::unique(*[]._type)} and no token, at most 2 datasets; never document contents
done: The dataset is private with a token for the site, or left public on purpose.
estimateChanges: A site that reads the dataset from the browser needs those queries moved to the server.

title: Your DMARC policy only watches
what: The domain's DMARC record has p=none: receiving servers report mail that fails, and deliver it anyway.
why: That is the right first step, and it doesn't stop anyone sending mail as you. Left at none, it never will.
fix: Read the DMARC reports for a few weeks, fix any service of yours that fails, then change p=none to p=quarantine (and later p=reject).
tech: Public DNS only: the TXT record at _dmarc.<host> starting v=DMARC1 has p=none; sp (the subdomain policy) does not change this
done: The DMARC policy moves from none to quarantine, then reject, after the reports look clean.
estimateChanges: The weeks spent reading reports and fixing each sender that fails.

title: Some events are missing details search engines need
what: An event in the page's structured data has no start date, no location or no event status.
why: Google needs these to show the event in results, and the status is how a cancelled or moved night is shown as such.
fix: Give every Event a startDate, a location and an eventStatus (for example https://schema.org/EventScheduled).
tech: Event JSON-LD without startDate, location or eventStatus (one finding listing each event and what it lacks)
done: Every Event has a startDate, a location and an eventStatus.
estimateChanges: Events entered by hand are edited one by one.

title: Two menu links report the same click
what: Two links to the same page, under different parent menus, send identical event values, so the report can't tell which one was clicked.
why: A comparison of a new menu is only real if every link reports where it sits: identical values merge the two links into one row.
fix: Add the parent menu (or another value that tells them apart) to the event both links send.
tech: Links that passed events-fire, grouped by destination: two with different parent menus whose events carry the same values for the plan's parameters. Needs a rendered read (G39): until then it is could not check
done: The two menu links report different events, told apart by the parent menu.
estimateChanges: One shared menu component is one edit.

title: Several form services on one page
what: Forms or form scripts from more than one service (for example HubSpot and Typeform) are on the same page.
why: Leads from one page end up in different places, and each service needs its own tracking, consent and follow-up.
fix: Check that each form is meant to be there, and move the page to one service if you can.
tech: Sightings of more than one of Pardot, Web-to-Lead, HubSpot, Formstack, Marketo and Typeform on one page (form action, iframe src, embed script); the tracking code alone is not a sighting
done: Each form on the page is meant to be there, or the page uses one service.
estimateChanges: Moving forms to one service means rebuilding each of them.

title: A hidden section is past its launch date
what: Today is after the launch date set for a hidden section, and gaugeline.hidden.json still lists it as hidden.
why: Either the launch slipped and nobody updated the plan, or it launched and the hidden checks are now guarding the wrong thing.
fix: Move the until date, or remove the section from gaugeline.hidden.json now that it's live.
tech: A hidden section's until date (YYYY-MM-DD, the whole day in UTC) is before the run's clock; no request is made
done: The until date is moved, or the section is removed from gaugeline.hidden.json.
estimateChanges: One entry in one file.

title: Some language codes are not valid
what: hreflang uses a code that isn't a valid language tag (such as "sp" or "es_US"), or a page with three or more languages has no x-default.
why: Search engines ignore an hreflang with an invalid code, and without x-default they guess which version to show everyone else.
fix: Use BCP 47 codes such as es, es-US or es-419 (a hyphen, not an underscore), and add hreflang="x-default" for the version to show when no language matches.
tech: an hreflang value is not a BCP 47 tag (two-letter languages must be ISO 639-1), or 3+ distinct languages have no x-default
done: Every hreflang value is a valid code such as es-US, with an x-default.
estimateChanges: A plugin that writes the codes may need a setting changed.

title: Some images have no alt attribute
what: Some images have no alt attribute at all, not even an empty one.
why: Without alt, screen readers read the file name aloud. An empty alt="" tells them to skip a decorative image; a missing one does not.
fix: Add alt to every img: a short description, or alt="" for decorative images.
tech: img elements with no alt attribute (one finding with a count and the first three)
done: Every img has an alt attribute: a description, or alt="" for decoration.
estimateChanges: Images inside CMS content are edited one by one.

title: Images use older, heavier file formats
what: Images are served as JPEG, PNG or GIF with no WebP or AVIF version offered.
why: WebP and AVIF are usually a quarter to a half smaller for the same picture, so the page loads faster.
fix: Offer WebP or AVIF with a <picture> element or srcset, or let your image CDN or framework image component pick the format.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Type is image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and it has no WebP or AVIF candidate (SVG is never reported)
done: Images are offered as WebP or AVIF through a picture element, srcset or the image component.
estimateChanges: A site with no image pipeline needs one set up first.

title: A language version declares the wrong language
what: A version's <html lang> names a different language than the version is (for example the Spanish page still says lang="en").
why: Screen readers read the page with the wrong voice and pronunciation, and browsers offer to translate it into its own language.
fix: Set <html lang> per version from the page's language, usually in the layout component.
tech: <html lang>'s primary subtag differs from the version's language (from hreflang or the configured scheme)
done: Each version's html lang matches the language of its content.
estimateChanges: One layout component usually sets it for every version.

title: Some text wasn't translated
what: Strings you listed as default-language text (button labels, headings) appear on another language version.
why: A Spanish page with an English "Add to cart" button looks unfinished, and some visitors won't know what it does.
fix: Translate the strings in the components that render them; they are usually hard-coded in a shared button or heading.
tech: a string from untranslated in gaugeline.languages.json appears in another version's main text or link names (case ignored); needs the list
done: The strings that were left in the other language are translated.
estimateChanges: Strings hard-coded in shared components are found and moved to the translations, then translated by someone who knows the language.

title: Some links don't say where they go
what: Links whose whole text is "read more", "click here", "learn more" or "here".
why: Screen reader users often browse a page by its links, and hear a list of identical "read more"s. Search engines also read link text to understand the destination.
fix: Make the link text name the destination, such as "Read more about pricing", or add an aria-label that does.
tech: a link's accessible name (aria-label, else its text) is exactly "read more", "click here", "learn more", "here" (English list)
done: Each link's text names its destination, or carries an aria-label that does.
estimateChanges: A shared button component used everywhere is one edit.

title: Links on this page go through a redirect
what: Links to other pages on the site answer with a redirect (3xx) before reaching the page.
why: Each redirect adds a round trip for visitors, and search engines pass a little less on through every hop.
fix: Change the link to the address it ends up at. This usually follows a move to new URLs, https or www.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] answers 3xx first and ends in 200
done: Each link goes to the address it ends up at.
estimateChanges: A move to new URLs changes every link at once, in the content as well as the templates.

title: One page has two names in your menus
what: The same link appears in the menu, header or footer with two different labels.
why: Visitors wonder whether the two labels are two pages, and the site reads as unfinished.
fix: Use one label for each page everywhere. Menus kept in two places (a header and a footer component) drift apart first.
tech: one href (a #fragment makes a different destination) has more than one distinct label across nav, header and footer (case and trailing arrows ignored)
done: Each page has one name in every menu.
estimateChanges: Menus kept in two components are edited twice.

title: Shared links have no picture
what: The page has no og:image tag.
why: When the page is shared in a chat or a social post, it shows as a plain link with no picture, which fewer people click.
fix: Add <meta property="og:image" content="https://..."> with a 1200 by 630 picture for the page.
tech: no og:image (or og:image:url) meta property
done: The page has an og:image with a full address, about 1200 by 630 pixels.
estimateChanges: Making the pictures is the cost if none exist.

title: A price changed since the last run
what: A product's price in the page's structured data is different from the last run's.
why: Sometimes that is the plan. When it isn't (a sync from the shop, an edit to the wrong product), customers and search results see the wrong price.
fix: If the change wasn't meant, correct the price at its source (the shop or CMS) and rebuild; if it was, nothing to do.
tech: With --since last only: the JSON-LD Offer price (integer minor units; anything but 48 or 48.00 is unread) for a product key (sku or name plus currency) present in both runs
done: The price is corrected at its source and the site rebuilt, or the change is accepted as meant.
estimateChanges: A price kept in several places is edited in each.

title: Breadcrumbs don't start where your guide says
what: The first item of a page's breadcrumb structured data is not the Home name and address your schema guide sets.
why: Search results show the breadcrumb trail; one that starts somewhere else on some pages looks inconsistent and can point at the wrong page.
fix: Start every BreadcrumbList with the configured first item, for example Home at /.
tech: the lowest-position ListItem's name or URL differs from breadcrumbs.firstName / breadcrumbs.firstUrl in gaugeline.schema.json (name case ignored, URL resolved)
done: Every BreadcrumbList starts with the configured first item.
estimateChanges: A shared breadcrumb component is one edit.

title: A phone link may not dial correctly
what: A tel: link has spaces or brackets in the number.
why: Some phones and click-to-call tools dial the wrong number, or nothing, when the link has spaces or brackets.
fix: Write the link as digits with a leading + and country code, for example href="tel:+14155550100". Keep the spaced format in the visible text only.
tech: an a[href^="tel:"] contains a space, ( or ); "-" and "." pass. One finding per distinct number
done: Each tel: link is digits with a leading + and country code.
estimateChanges: Links typed into content are one edit each.

title: A temporary address doesn't name the real one
what: The page is served from a hosting provider's temporary address and has no canonical tag.
why: If a search engine finds the temporary address, nothing tells it the real page is on your domain, and the preview can show up in results.
fix: Add <link rel="canonical" href="https://yourdomain/..."> to every page, so each preview points at the real address.
tech: The final address's host ends in .vercel.app, .netlify.app or .pages.dev and the HTML has no link rel=canonical
done: Every page on the temporary host has a canonical pointing at the real domain.
estimateChanges: A shared layout is one edit.

title: Invisible characters sit inside words on the page
what: Zero-width characters are inside words in the page's visible text.
why: A word with a hidden character in it no longer matches itself: search can't find it, and copy-pasted or tampered text can carry marks nobody meant to publish.
fix: Remove them from the source text: retype the word, or paste it as plain text.
tech: U+200B to U+200D, U+2060 to U+2064, U+180E or U+FEFF between two Latin, Cyrillic, Greek or digit characters in visible text; emoji joiners, Persian non-joiners and zero-width marks at the end of a text (content source maps) are not counted
done: The invisible characters are removed from the words they sit inside.
estimateChanges: The number of fields they came from. Text pasted from a word processor often repeats the problem.

title: A redirect drops the old address's query string
what: An old address with a query string redirects to an address without it.
why: Campaign tags and filters on old links are lost, so their visits can't be told apart.
fix: Pass the query string on in the redirect rule.
tech: The legacy address has a query; the trail's final address has none
done: The redirect passes the query string on.
estimateChanges: One rule is one edit. Several rules each need it.

title: Addresses in the rank export are neither live nor planned
what: Pages in the --rank export (Search Console or a rank tracker) are neither in the --live list nor in the plan.
why: Usually the export is of another site or property, or of pages already gone: the numbers on the uncovered list may not be the site's.
fix: Check the export is of this site's property and recent, or add the pages to --live if they still exist.
tech: Export paths (the --live key: lower case, no trailing slash, no query or host) not in the set of live paths or row paths. One finding with the count and three examples
done: The rank export is of this site and recent, or the missing pages are added to --live.
estimateChanges: Getting a fresh export from the search tool.

title: One page's primary keyword is another page's secondary
what: A page's Primary Keyword is also listed as a Secondary Keyword of other pages.
why: Often deliberate, supporting pages in a cluster; worth a look, because a strong supporting page can outrank the page meant to win the term.
fix: Check the supporting pages link to the primary page, and that none of them is built to rank for the term itself.
tech: Each Secondary Keyword cell is split on commas, semicolons and line breaks and compared like primaries. Reported from the primary's side, only when one page has the term as its primary
done: The supporting pages link to the primary page and none is built to rank for its term.
estimateChanges: Content edits on each supporting page.

title: A printed address takes more than two redirects
what: A printed address takes more than two redirects to land.
why: Every hop is a wait on a phone, often on a weak signal, and one broken hop breaks the code.
fix: Redirect the printed address straight to its page.
tech: More than two 3xx in the trail; the trail is in the evidence
done: The printed address redirects once, straight to its page.
estimateChanges: Rules in a short-link service, the host and the app each need checking.

title: An email has no plain-text version
what: An .html email has no .txt file with the same name beside it, and gaugeline.emails.json says every email should have one.
why: A message with only an HTML part is more likely to be treated as bulk mail, and anyone whose mail client shows text only, or reads aloud, gets nothing.
fix: Export or write the plain-text version (order.html and order.txt), and send both as one multipart message.
tech: only when gaugeline.emails.json sets "textVersion": true; an .html or .htm email with no .txt of the same name in the same folder (order.es.html wants order.es.txt); without that setting the check says it could not run and passes nothing
done: Each .html email has a .txt with the same name beside it, and the export writes both.
estimateChanges: Most email tools export a plain-text version with one option. A hand-written template needs the text written.

title: A page marked static is never served from the CDN's cache
what: A page you marked static in gaugeline.cost.json was a cache miss on both of two visits a few seconds apart.
why: A page that is meant to be the same for everyone should be built once and served from the CDN. When every visit is a miss, the host does the work every time, which costs money and makes the page slower.
fix: Look for what opts the page out of the cache: a Cache-Control of no-store or private, a cookie or header the page reads, a fetch with cache: no-store, or a dynamic function. On Next.js, make the route static or give it a revalidate time.
tech: Only pages marked static ("static" in gaugeline.cost.json: a path or a "/folder/*"). Two GETs about 3 seconds apart, no cookies. The cache state is read from x-vercel-cache (HIT, STALE, PRERENDER, REVALIDATED are hits; MISS, BYPASS misses), cf-cache-status (HIT, STALE, UPDATING, REVALIDATED; MISS, EXPIRED, BYPASS, DYNAMIC) and a positive Age; a hit on either visit passes. A response with none of those is could-not-check, not a guess. When a lifetime of a second or more explains the misses, revalidate-too-often is reported instead
done: The page's second visit is served from the CDN's cache (a hit), so the host does not build it for every visitor.
estimateChanges: Usually a cache header or a revalidate setting, an hour. More when something the page reads (a cookie, a header, a no-store fetch) opts it out of the cache.

title: A page marked static is rebuilt too often
what: A page you marked static sends a cache lifetime shorter than the minimum you set (60 seconds unless you changed it).
why: A lifetime of a second or two means the host rebuilds the page about as often as it is visited. A page that changes once a day does not need that, and every rebuild is billed.
fix: Raise the lifetime to what the content needs: an hour for a menu, a day for an about page. On Next.js that is the revalidate setting; on any host it is the s-maxage in Cache-Control.
tech: Only pages marked static ("static" in gaugeline.cost.json). The lifetime is s-maxage when Cache-Control has one, else max-age; no-store, no-cache and private count as zero. A max-age with no s-maxage is the browser's lifetime: when the CDN answered a hit (Vercel and Cloudflare keep such a page until the next deploy or purge) it is fine. Compared with "minimumSeconds" (default 60). A page with no Cache-Control header is could-not-check. A zero lifetime on a page that never hit the cache is reported as never-cached instead
done: The page's cache lifetime is at least the minimum in gaugeline.cost.json (60 seconds by default), so the host keeps a copy instead of rebuilding it.
estimateChanges: Minutes: a number in a revalidate setting or a header. Decide with the client how stale a page may be.

title: Trackers load on a page with a form or a listed path
what: Gaugeline lists the advertising pixels, analytics, session replay tools and tag managers that load on a page with a form, an embedded form service or a path you listed as sensitive, with the id each one carries.
why: A form or a page about a health condition, a booking or an intake is where visitors share details, and anything that loads there can receive information about the visit. Clients are often surprised to find what the site loads. This is a list of facts: whether any of it is allowed is for the client and their own counsel to decide, and Gaugeline does not say.
fix: Show the client the list. For each tracker, ask who set it up and what it is for; where it is not needed on this page, move it out of the page template or restrict it in the tag manager. For the question of whether a tracker is allowed here, the client should ask their own counsel.
tech: Only with --trackers. A page counts when it has a form that collects details (a search box, a GET form whose visible fields are named like a search, does not count), an embedded form service, or a path listed under "sensitivePaths" in gaugeline.trackers.json. Trackers are read from the script addresses and inline scripts in the HTML (and the noscript fallback tags) by a fixed table of patterns: Meta pixel, TikTok pixel, LinkedIn Insight Tag, Google Analytics 4, Google Tag Manager, five session replay tools (Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, FullStory, LogRocket, Mouseflow) and the tracking code of HubSpot, Pardot and Marketo. Each finding shows the kind and the id the page's own code carries, never page content or a form field. A tag a script adds after the page loads is not seen (a run that fires scripts is a later branch); the same page gives the same findings
done: The client has seen the list of trackers on this page, with their ids, and has decided with their own counsel which stay; running Gaugeline again shows the list they chose.
estimateChanges: An hour to go through the list with the client. More when a tag manager adds trackers that have to be taken out one by one, or the form service's own tracking cannot be turned off.

title: A Tag Manager container on a page with a form or a listed path holds trackers
what: A Google Tag Manager container loads on a page with a form, an embedded form service or a path you listed as sensitive, and its public file contains tracker ids (Meta, TikTok, LinkedIn, session replay, Google Analytics 4).
why: A tag manager hides what the page loads: the page's own code shows one container id, and the trackers are inside it. They are the same kind of fact as the ones in the page's code, and the same question for the client and their own counsel. Gaugeline lists them and does not say whether any is allowed.
